desc: draft CPD review - Congo - Climate
full: Dear Global Practice and Cross Sectoral Teams: I would like to share with you the first draft of Congo’s CPD for your review. It's important to note that the CPD draft for the Congo country office is the only CPD and CEP from WCAR scheduled for submission to the Executive Board in February 2027. For the purpose of kickstarting the review process, we would like to clarify the nature of the contributions from CoE for the review of this first draft of the CPD. All technical comments and proposed edits are to be recorded directly to the draft CDP (documents uploaded) : All review and commenting to be completed by Tuesday, 1 st September Consolidated feedback to the Congo office: Wednesday 2 nd September We are aware that many of you have been working closely with your counterparts at the Country Office level over the past few months, including during the SMR process. Therefore, we encourage you to focus your review on any major strategic issues or challenges identified in the document and share your observations with us via email. To streamline the consolidation process, please send your feedback to Nadia Noor in the Regional PMD team, and we will ensure that it is incorporated into the consolidated feedback provided to the Country Office. In addition, we recommend that strategic observations and recommendations be included as needed, with at least two substantive points per section where relevant.

desc: CPD development (SMR) - Nigeria - ESP
full: On behalf of WCARO, I would like to submit a Technical Assistance request for support from the Centres of Excellence (CoE) to UNICEF Nigeria as part of the development of its 2028–2032 Country Programme and the preparation of its first Strategic Moment of Reflection (SMR), scheduled for 8–10 September 2026 . The SMR will support the Country Office in assessing the evolving situation of children, identifying key deprivations, inequities and implementation bottlenecks, and defining the strategic intent and priority areas for the next Country Programme. The Country Office has also expressed interest in continued technical engagement following the SMR, particularly during the development of the Theory of Change and related CPD design processes. The requested areas of expertise include: Health (health systems strengthening, newborn mortality, immunization and zero-dose children); WASH; Climate Change and Disaster Risk Reduction; Nutrition; Education; Child Protection; Social Policy and Livelihoods/Economic Opportunities; Social and Behaviour Change (SBC); Gender Equality and Disability Inclusion; Youth Engagement (GenU); Supply The Country Office has proposed a number of preferred experts from the CoE; however, we fully understand that the final allocation will be determined based on availability and GPD considerations. A copy of the original request and proposed profiles is attached for reference. We would appreciate GPD's assessment of this request and support in identifying the most appropriate resource persons to accompany Nigeria through this important phase of the CPD process. Many thanks in advance for your support and collaboration.

desc: CPD development - Kenya - ESP
full: CPD 2027-2032 development support (multi-sector) Request type: Technical assistance from the Centre of Excellence for the development of the UNICEF Kenya Country Programme Document 2027–2032. Background: UNICEF Kenya is initiating development of its next Country Programme Document for 2027–2032. The process will require focused technical support at key moments, including strategic framing, theory of change and strategy development, and review of draft programme documentation. The objective is to ensure that the new CPD is evidence-informed, strategically coherent, aligned with national priorities and UNICEF corporate guidance, and responsive to emerging risks and opportunities for children and adolescents in Kenya. The Kenya CPD will be approved at the June 2027 Board. Requested Support 1. Analysis, Theory of Change and strategy development — early to mid-September We request targeted CoE support for theory of change and strategy development for selected key themes and sectors where additional technical guidance would be most useful. This support would involve a few days of engagement with UNICEF Kenya sector teams in late August to mid-September, helping teams translate the framing analysis into clearer programme choices, causal pathways, strategic shifts and results logic. This work involves initial conversations with the prorgamme teams, then in person participation as follows: Wednesday 9 Sep – Education Thursday 10 Sep – CSD 1 (health, nutrition, WASH) Friday 11 Sep (half day) – CSD 2 (health, nutrition, WASH) Monday 14 Sep – CP Tuesday 15 Sep – SP Level of effort: several days of engagement with selected sector teams. 2. Strategic consultation meeting — 30 September We request CoE support for a half-day strategic consultation meeting in late September (30 th ), to review the evolving situation of children and adolescents in Kenya and identify the key strategic issues that should shape the CPD. This is with the resident Coordinator and his office, some UN agencies, and RO and COE staff. We would ideally like several COE technical colleagues to support the discussion, covering: social policy; strategic planning; climate and resilience; youth and adolescents; health; education; and child protection. In-person participation would be preferred where feasible, with remote participation possible for some sectors, such as education and child protection. Level of effort: half-day meeting, with preparation time as needed. 3. Document review and quality assurance — timing to be confirmed, likely late September into October. We also request technical review of draft CPD-related materials (e.g. Explanatory Notes) across UNICEF Kenya’s six programme sectors and cross-cutting issues, including whether sector strategies, theories of change, explanatory notes and related inputs are technically sound, coherent across sectors, and adequately reflect priorities such as equity, gender, disability inclusion, climate resilience, adolescent and youth engagement, and systems strengthening. Level of effort: approximately two to three days per reviewer or technical area, depending on the number of documents and depth of comments required. This is created for Mahboob Bajwa (Dep Rep Programmes); but would need to loop in James Hedges jhedges@unicef.org (Chief PME) as well as ESARO Chief PPM Behzad Noubary <bnoubary@unicef.org>.

desc: Support integration of climate and DRR into the new India Country Programme Document.
full: CoE focal points: Aashima Garg < agarg@unicef.org >; Benjamin Schreiber < bschreiber@unicef.org >; Chemba Raghavan < craghavan@unicef.org >; Christine Hofer < chofer@unicef.org >; Deepak Bhaskaran < dbhaskaran@unicef.org >; Francis Odhiambo < fodhiambo@unicef.org >; Glayson Dos Santos < gdossantos@unicef.org >; Gopal Mitra < gmitra@unicef.org >; James McQuen Patterson < jmcquenpatterson@unicef.org >; Jane Mwangi < jmwangi@unicef.org >; Kirsten Di Martino < kdimartino@unicef.org >; Lauren Whitehead < lwhitehead@unicef.org >; Mekiya Feki < mfeki@unicef.org >; Mitsue Uemura < muemura@unicef.org >; Nangar Soomro < nsoomro@unicef.org >; Neha Kapil < nkapil@unicef.org >; Ratna Jhaveri < rjhaveri@unicef.org >; Saadgi Sanjay Rajani < srajani@unicef.org >; Samson Muradzikwa < smuradzikwa@unicef.org >; Satvika Chalasani < schalasani@unicef.org >; Shreyasi Jha < sjha@unicef.org >; Sunita Joergensen < sjoergensen@unicef.org > Title: Country Programme Development TA – India CO Background UNICEF India is developing its next Country Programme Document (CPD) 2028-2032. Following completion of the evidence synthesis, prioritization exercise, and SMR1, the Country Office seeks coordinated technical assistance from GPD and Centres of Excellence (CoEs) to support the next phases of CPD development, ensuring a focused, differentiated, equity-driven and financially realistic programme aligned with UNICEF's Strategic Plan and FSID approach. Priority Programme and Cross-Sectoral Areas for TA Child Survival and Development Education Child Protection Social Policy and Child Poverty Climate Resilience and Environment Gender Equality Disability Inclusion Adolescents and Youth Engagement Social and Behaviour Change Data, Evidence and Monitoring Systems Strengthening South-South and Triangular Cooperation (SSTC) Digital Transformation and Innovation Technical Assistance Requested 1. Prioritization Follow-up (Post-SMR1) (Written feedback from CoE colleagues was requested by 3 August , as indicated in the email circulated on 30 July from APRO ) Review and validate prioritization logic. Provide technical feedback on selected manifestations/deprivations. Advise on comparative advantage, differentiation, and strategic choices. Challenge and strengthen trade-off analysis and focus decisions. 2. Theory of Change Development Support development of integrated and cross-sectoral theories of change. Identify systems bottlenecks, leverage points and pathways to scale. Ensure alignment with FSID (Focus, Scale & Impact, Differentiation). Strengthen articulation of programmatic and systems transformation strategies. 3. Results and Resources Planning Review outcome and output architecture. Advise on results framework design and prioritization. Support resource realism and strategic investment choices. Ensure coherence between manifestation, strategies, outputs and indicators. 4. Draft CPD Review Technical review of CPD narrative. Validation of strategic positioning and comparative advantage. Review for equity, gender, disability and climate integration. Quality assurance of coherence across CPD components. 5. Cross-Cutting Strategic Advice Equity-focused programming and last-mile delivery approaches. Systems strengthening and institutional capacity development. Scale and sustainability considerations. South-South and Triangular Cooperation opportunities. Private sector engagement and innovative financing approaches. Digital, AI and data-driven programming opportunities. Expected Deliverables Technical review comments on SMR, ToC, RRP and CPD drafts. If you have any questions related to CPD development, please contact Christopher Gill. Country Programme Development TA – Republic of Kyrgyzstan (2028–2032) The Kyrgyzstan CO requests technical assistance from the Centres of Excellence and GPD to support the development of the next CP following the RO-endorsed CPD roadmap. The CO seeks strategic and technical support across priority programme and cross-sectoral areas that are emerging through the evidence generation and consultation process. These include: Child poverty and social protection, including public finance for children, universal child benefit implementation, shock-responsive social protection and demographic transition considerations. Health and nutrition, with particular focus on primary health care, immunization, maternal and child health, adolescent health, environmental health, nutrition financing and health system strengthening. Education and skills development, including foundational learning, digital learning transformation, inclusive education and learning-to-earning pathways. Child protection, including childcare reform, social service workforce strengthening, prevention of violence against children. Climate resilience and environmental sustainability, integrating climate adaptation and resilience across programme sectors. SBC, including community engagement and behaviour change approaches to support programme results. The CO requests technical support for key CP milestones and products, including: Development and refinement of ToC In person participation from some key experts at the TOC workshop planned in October Programme prioritization/identification of pathways to scale and impact RRF/RRP development Technical review of associated strategic documents and evidence products Participation in key milestone workshops and consultations, as required.

desc: CPD development products review - Tunisia - SBC
full: Subject: Request for Technical Review – UNICEF Tunisia Country Programme Document (CPD) 2027–2031 Dear colleagues, As part of the quality assurance process for the UNICEF Tunisia Country Programme Document (CPD) 2027–2031 , we would greatly appreciate your review of the enclosed CPD package, including the CPD, Programme Strategy Explanatory Notes (PSENs) comprising Theories of Change (ToCs), Results and Resources Plans (RRPs), and accompanying review matrix. The review package is available here: Review Package: TCO_CPD 2027-2031_Review Package Review Focus We would particularly welcome your views on: Executive Board sensitivity and strategic positioning Consistency with Strategic Moment of Reflection (SMR) decisions Quality and coherence of Theories of Change Convergence and causal linkages across outcomes and programme components Assumptions regarding UNICEF and partner contributions Adequacy, measurability and readiness of proposed indicators, including GMF indicators Timeline Please provide comments by 12 August 2026 . Feedback from Global Practice Groups, Cross-Sectoral Teams, Centres of Excellence and MENARO will be consolidated and addressed by the Country Office before final Regional Office review, Regional Director approval and submission to OSEB by 5 October 2026 . Comments may be provided either: Directly in the documents using tracked changes/comments; and/or As strategic observations and recommendations in the accompanying review matrix. We encourage reviewers to prioritize substantive and strategic observations over editorial comments. Background The proposed CPD has been developed drawing on: The Tunisia Evidence Synthesis (2025); The end-of-cycle review of the current programme; A country office-wide Visioning Exercise; Joint UN consultations undertaken for development of the UNSDCF 2027–2031 with Government, development partners, civil society, academia and other stakeholders; UNICEF-specific consultations with Government counterparts on the proposed programme architecture, results framework and strategic positioning, which are largely complete, with a final presentation and validation meeting with Government partners scheduled for the end of August 2026; The Strategic Moment of Reflection (SMR) conducted in January 2026 with the participation of the MENA Regional Director, Regional Office colleagues, Centres of Excellence and the Country Office, which helped define the strategic priorities, programme architecture and results structure. The current CPD 2021–2025 was extended through 2026 to enable alignment with the National Development Plan 2026–2030, the UNSDCF 2027–2031 and the above consultation processes. The new CPD reflects the strategic directions emerging from the SMR, including the principles of differentiation, focus, scale and impact, supported by a tiered prioritization methodology. Areas for Review 1. Strategic Positioning and Executive Board Readiness Please identify any language, positioning, assumptions or formulations that may raise concerns during Executive Board review, as well as areas where the rationale, evidence base or framing could be strengthened. 2. Consistency with the Strategic Moment of Reflection Please assess whether the CPD adequately reflects the strategic directions agreed during the SMR, including: Focus, differentiation, scale and impact; Strategic prioritization and selectivity; Convergence and cross-sectoral collaboration; Systems strengthening and pathways to scale; Upstream policy, governance and financing dimensions; The balance between continuity and innovation. 3. Alignment with UNICEF auditable and other organisational guidance Please review consistency with: The UNICEF Strategic Plan and Africa Strategy; Programme Strategy Explanatory Note guidance; Mandatory Theory of Change requirements; Results and Resources Plan requirements; Relevant Global Practice and Cross-Sectoral Team guidance. In particular, please assess whether outcome and output statements, results chains, assumptions and Theories of Change are coherent, evidence-based and sufficiently articulate causal pathways, including convergence across outcomes and programme components. 4. Adequacy of the Results Architecture and Measurement Framework Please review: Outcome and output logic; Consistency between the CPD, ToCs and RRPs; Adequacy and strategic value of proposed indicators; Indicator measurability and usefulness for accountability and learning; Readiness and methodological robustness of proposed GMF indicators, including definitions, methodologies, data sources and means of verification; Feasibility of establishing and tracking baselines and targets. 5. UNICEF Contribution and Partnerships Please assess whether the programme adequately articulates: UNICEF’s comparative advantage and contribution; The roles and expected contributions of Government and other partners; Key assumptions regarding partner engagement and capacity; Partnership strategies required to achieve results at scale. 6. Linkages Across Programme Components Please review whether the programme sufficiently captures: Convergence and synergies across programme components; Interdependencies and complementarities across outcomes; Opportunities for integrated programming and collective impact; Pathways through which combined sectoral interventions and UN joint programming contribute to higher-level change. Thank you in advance for your support and technical expertise in shaping UNICEF Tunisia’s next Country Programme. The Country Office looks forward to your comments and recommendations. With thanks and appreciation, UNICEF Tunisia Country Office

Technical Assistance Request: Alternative Care Governance and Data Sharing for Fostered Children in Oman Consultation with Vedasto Nsanzugwanko took place and review is underway. 1. Background and purpose The Ministry of Social Development (MoSD) has requested UNICEF Oman’s technical support to identify relevant good practices and legal approaches related to alternative care for children in foster families. The request follows discussions with foster families, during which challenges were raised regarding civil registry records, official documentation, and the ability of foster families to complete transactions or access services on behalf of fostered children, particularly children whose fathers are unknown. 2. Scope of support The technical assistance request is to provide a review of selected international, Arab, Gulf, and Muslim-majority country experiences to identify practical options for authorizing foster families to undertake official transactions in the child’s best interests, while safeguarding children’s rights, identity, privacy, and protection, and taking into account Oman’s legal and Sharia context. 3. Key areas of review Legal and regulatory frameworks on alternative care, foster care, guardianship, civil registration, and access to official records. Mechanisms for authorizing foster families or caregivers in official systems without compromising the child’s legal identity, rights, privacy, or protection. Data-sharing arrangements and safeguards between civil registration authorities, child protection authorities, social development entities, and authorized caregivers. Practical options relevant to Oman, including possible legal, administrative, or procedural adjustments. 4. Proposed deliverables A concise comparative technical note on selected country practices, legal approaches, and governance models. A short matrix of country examples covering legal basis, institutional arrangements, data-sharing mechanisms, safeguards, and relevance to Oman. An options note with practical recommendations for MoSD’s consideration. A technical discussion with MoSD and relevant stakeholders to review findings and agree on next steps. 5. Modality and expected use The support may be delivered through a desk review, consultation with UNICEF regional and global child protection and legal experts, and, where feasible, peer exchange with selected countries. The outputs will inform MoSD’s discussions with relevant national authorities on strengthening alternative care governance and ensuring that any adjustments to official records or data-sharing practices are child-centred, rights-based, legally sound, and contextually appropriate for Oman.

desc: Country visit on MAR and country programme
full: UNICEF Somalia is advancing a portfolio of WASH innovation and systems-strengthening work to improve climate-resilient water, sanitation and hygiene services in fragile and drought-affected contexts. A key area of work is the recharge Managed Aquifer Recharge (MAR) programme in Dolow, which has so far focused primarily on field-level activities and implementation. While this has generated important operational learning, engagement with Jubaland-level authorities in Kismayo has been limited and now requires greater attention to institutionalize MAR, clarify regional ownership and management arrangements, and create the conditions for sustainable scale-up. Esther Shaylor, WASH Innovation Manager in the UNICEF Innovation team, part of the Centre of Excellence (CoE) WASH and country focal for Somalia, will visit Mogadishu and Dollow to support two complementary areas of work. For the Innovation work, the visit will focus on reviewing progress and implementation needs for MAR in Dolow, identifying what is required to move from field implementation toward sustainable management, and proposing the next phase of stakeholder engagement at the federal and regional level. In her role as CoE WASH country focal, the visit will provide an opportunity to engage the UNICEF Somalia WASH team on strategic planning, better understand current and emerging programme priorities, and identify the type of future technical assistance and support required from the CoE to strengthen the country programme over time.

desc: Support to governance (roadmap), capacity strengthening, and use of geospatial analyses for microplanning and equity.
full: The Country Office and the DHx CoE have agreed to pursue geospatial technical assistance focused on two priority entry points: immunization and vaccination microplanning, and community health. The geospatial component sits within the broader TA request submitted to the CoE, which also covers DHIS2/SNIS optimization, eCHIS, campaign digitalization, interoperability, and data governance, but is treated as a distinct workstream given its specific technical and political sensitivities. For immunization, the geospatial support is expected to address gaps in identifying under-vaccinated or zero-dose villages, tracking vaccination team movements during campaigns, estimating target populations including nomadic groups, and visualizing low-coverage zones to guide catch-up planning. For community health, the focus is on geolocating community health workers to verify home visit completion, mapping households at community level, and supporting real-time postnatal and neonatal follow-up given the country's high neonatal mortality rate. The type of digital health solution discussed is largely an extension and strengthening of existing tools rather than a new platform. The CO already uses ODK for geographic coordinate collection and QGIS for basic spatial analysis and heat maps, but describes both as underdeveloped. No new platform commitment has been made; the meeting notes point toward improving data quality, analytical capacity, and integration of geospatial outputs with existing systems (e-Santé COM, DHIS2, the immunization registry) rather than introducing new infrastructure.

desc: Resource mobilization and programme sustainability
full: 3. Resource mobilization and programme sustainability While we have secured funding for few climate initiatives, additional resource mobilization support will be critical to sustain and scale the programme, particularly to expand climate resilience across sectors. We would particularly appreciate the Climate CoE's support in advocating for the inclusion of Senegal in the GCF proposal Climate Facilities for Children (CF4C) , as this could provide an important opportunity to scale our work. At the same time, given the uncertainty around the GCF pipeline, we would welcome support in identifying and exploring alternative climate finance opportunities should the current GCF proposal not move forward. The Climate Specialist position is currently funded only until June 2027. Given the size of the Country Office and the fact that climate programming is currently led by a single staff member, this represents a significant risk to programme continuity. Support in identifying sustainable funding for both the programme and the position would be greatly appreciated.

desc: Introduce UNICEF Turkmenistan's climate action programming under the new CPD 2026-2030 and discuss youth and green skills priorities.
full: CO would like to introduce themselves and present UNICEF Turkmenistan’s achievements to date, and share key priorities under the Country Programme Document (CPD) 2026–2030, where climate action is recognized as a strategic priority. Under the climate action and youth flagship area, the new programme of cooperation aims to significantly increase the number of children and young people equipped with climate adaptation and DRR knowledge and skills, while promoting sustainable “green” behaviours. These efforts are fully aligned with the country’s 2030 Agenda commitments, the National Climate Change Strategy, the National Action Plan for Realization of Children’s Rights (2023-2028), and the NDC. A key component is the expansion of the national “Green School” initiative — jointly launched with the Ministry of Education in 2025 — with plans to reach 500 schools by 2030. Given the ambition of the current programme cycle and current resource mobilization needs in climate action, the CO would value the opportunity to explore potential areas of alignment and discuss whether submission of a concept note under the CEED thematic pool (2026–2029 funding window) may be feasible.

desc: The strategic purpose of this request is to lay the foundation for integrated VAC prevention and response programme management
full: The strategic purpose of this request is to lay the foundation for integrated VAC prevention and response programme management. Addressing VAC in BiH requires moving beyond fragmented, sectoral, project-based interventions. Thus support is needed to establish programme management structure within the CO with identifying entry points, including catalytic policy and financing. The goal is to shift from siloed interventions to integrated, system-wide programming. UNICEF BiH seeks support in designing and operationalizing VAC related interventions, including programme design for high impact violence prevention solutions. CoE support is requested to conduct a scoping analysis of VAC policy environment, coordination structures, and delivery mechanisms. The TA would guide the design of a cross sectoral operational framework, define roles, propose budget lines and financing options, and develop a monitoring and learning agenda. Special attention should be given to integrating VAC work with the implementation of the European Child Guarantee, de-institutionalization reform, educational, and juvenile justice programmes. This technical support will be very timely also in light of the planned recruitment of a Child Protection Specialist in January 2026 in laying the groundwork for a more cohesive and strategic VAC portfolio, addressing current fragmentation and enabling UNICEF to engage holistically in this critical area

desc: Transform juvenile justice systems to prioritize prevention, diversion, and rehabilitation through child-sensitive, rights-based approaches
full: Technical assistance is required to re-design and institutionalize a child-sensitive juvenile justice framework that embeds prevention, diversion, and rehabilitation as core principles. It will also guide the creation of structured diversion programs, community-based rehabilitation services, and capacity-building plans for justice and social welfare actors. By integrating these reforms into policy and practice, the assistance will deliver a sustainable system that protects children’s rights, reduces recidivism, and strengthens cross-sector collaboration for holistic child protection.

desc: High-level advocacy and legal review to safeguard child rights, including draft law analysis and standards on minimum age of criminal responsibility.

desc: Evaluate and renew national strategies to end child marriage through evidence-based, system-level reform
full: Technical support for a multisectoral evaluation of the National Strategy to End Child Marriage (2017–2024), and in a second phase, support for the development of a new national strategy, elevating attention and action on a persisting issue requiring attention. (Policy Reform and Programme Design) UNICEF Madagascar is requesting technical assistance to support the evaluation of the National Strategy on Ending Child Marriage (2017–2024). The implementation of the strategy faced a number of challenges, making a thorough evaluation essential before the development of a new strategy. During this period, the prevalence of girls aged 20–24 who were married before the age of 18 increased from 39% in 2018 to 42% in 2025, underscoring the need for sustained and strengthened national action. This includes continued multisectoral engagement and, based on the findings of the evaluation, the development of a new national strategy, with the mobilisation of key partners, including UNFPA.

desc: Transform juvenile justice systems to prioritize prevention, diversion, and rehabilitation through child-sensitive, rights-based approaches
full: 2.Juvenile Justice System Reform: Strengthening Prevention, Diversion, and Rehabilitation for Children in Conflict with the Law This initiative aims to transform the juvenile justice system into a child-sensitive, rights-based framework that prioritizes prevention, diversion, and rehabilitation over punitive measures. The strategic purpose is to reduce the criminalization of children and ensure compliance with international standards, while addressing root causes of offending behavior. The intended system-level change is the institutionalization of integrated mechanisms—policy, protocols, and services—that enable early intervention, community-based alternatives, and structured rehabilitation programs. This reform will strengthen coordination among justice, social welfare, and education sectors, ensuring sustainable, scalable solutions that protect children’s rights and promote reintegration into society. Technical assistance is required to re-design and institutionalize a child-sensitive juvenile justice framework that embeds prevention, diversion, and rehabilitation as core principles. This support will help develop national standards, operational guidelines, and inter-agency coordination mechanisms to replace punitive approaches with restorative practices. It will also guide the creation of structured diversion programs, community-based rehabilitation services, and capacity-building plans for justice and social welfare actors. By integrating these reforms into policy and practice, the assistance will deliver a sustainable system that protects children’s rights, reduces recidivism, and strengthens cross-sector collaboration for holistic child protection.

desc: Institutionalize technology-enabled prevention and early intervention within national child protection systems
full: A system-strengthening initiative to institutionalize technology-enabled prevention and early intervention services within national child protection systems. This includes digitizing Risiha assessment and case management tools and transitioning ParentText/ParentApp to government ownership. Embedding digitized Risiha tools into government and organisational service delivery will enable timely identification of risks, consistent monitoring, and improved targeting of support for vulnerable children and families. Concurrently, establishing governance and technical capacity for ParentText/ParentApp will ensure sustainability and scale-up of evidence-based digital parenting support. Together, these actions will reinforce national delivery of family-strengthening interventions to prevent violence in homes and communities. Technical assistance is required to design and implement the digitization of Risiha tools, including technical specifications, integration with provincial and national IMS, data standards, workflows, and quality assurance. Additional support is needed to guide the government-led pathway to ownership of ParentText/ParentApp, covering governance structures, content stewardship, costed implementation plans, data protection protocols, and long-term systems integration. This assistance will build national capacity to sustain and scale both platforms, ensuring they function as core components of child protection systems for prevention and early intervention.

desc: Scale justice for children from pilot initiatives to a national system
full: Scaling up justice for children – from pilot to national model UNICEF is currently implementing an integrated service package for justice for children in one major urban area (Kandy). By end-Q1 2026, the first six months of implementation of this pilot will provide operational evidence to assess functionality, gaps, and system-readiness for expansion. UNICEF will need to assess and use that evidence to propose a cost-efficient pathway for sustainable scale-up nationwide. This will likely include adjusting institutional responsibilities, refining the model based on early lessons, and developing a scalable financing and workforce approach. The specifics—appropriate sequencing, cost implications, and political feasibility—will become clearer once early performance data and feedback is analysed with UNICEF’s aim being to ensure that a realistic, evidence-based scale-up plan is on the table for government consideration by Q2/Q3 to feed into the preparation of the 2027 budget planning process.

desc: Climate finance and GCF technical assistance to support climate‑resilient WASH and water resources management
full: This technical assistance will provide specialized support to develop climate‑resilient WASH investment concepts and proposals, with a focus on Green Climate Fund (GCF) and other climate finance mechanisms. Support will include preparation of concept notes and full proposals; articulation of climate rationale, adaptation pathways, theories of change, budgets, and co‑financing strategies; and alignment with national climate priorities. The TA will integrate climate‑sensitive water resources management considerations and support compliance with climate finance requirements, including environmental and social safeguards.

desc: Technical assistance to integrate climate‑sensitive water resources management into WASH programming
full: This technical assistance will support UNICEF Yemen to strengthen the integration of climate‑sensitive water resources management (WRM) into WASH programme design, planning, and investment decisions. The TA will focus on improving the sustainability and resilience of groundwater‑dependent water supply systems by incorporating water availability assessments, climate risk screening of water sources, sustainable abstraction principles, and basic groundwater protection measures into WASH programming. The assistance will help embed WRM considerations into technical designs, programme strategies, and planning tools, ensuring that WASH investments are aligned with long‑term water resource availability and climate resilience objectives. The TA will also provide technical guidance to support informed decision‑making in severely water‑scarce and climate‑stressed contexts, contributing to reduced risks of over‑abstraction, system failure, and unintended negative impacts on water resources. Expected Outputs / Deliverables: Practical guidance for integrating WRM into WASH programme design Climate‑risk screening inputs for water supply interventions Strengthened alignment between WASH investments and water resource sustainability Enhanced technical capacity of staff and partners on WRM‑WASH linkages

desc: Technical assistance on solarization and sustainability of water and sanitation systems under Yemen CPD 2027–2029
full: This technical assistance will provide specialized support to strengthen the design, sustainability, and climate resilience of water and sanitation systems through appropriate solarization and energy‑efficient technologies. The TA will focus on reducing reliance on fuel‑based systems, improving service continuity, and strengthening operation and maintenance (O&M) models for water supply and sanitation infrastructure in fragile and resource‑constrained contexts. Support will include technical review and guidance on solar‑powered water supply systems, energy needs assessment, system sizing, lifecycle costing, and performance standards. In addition, the TA will provide technical inputs to improve the sustainability of sanitation systems, including wastewater management and fecal sludge treatment facilities, where energy requirements affect functionality and long‑term operation. The assistance will ensure that solarization contributes to climate mitigation and adaptation objectives while improving technical quality, cost‑effectiveness, and durability of WASH services. Expected Outputs / Deliverables: Technical guidance on solar‑powered water supply systems Improved design and sustainability of energy‑dependent sanitation infrastructure Lifecycle costing and O&M recommendations for solarized WASH systems Strengthened technical capacity of staff and partners on solarization and sustainability

desc: Technical assistance to strengthen sanitation and fecal sludge management (FSM) system
full: This technical assistance will provide specialized support to strengthen sanitation and fecal sludge management (FSM) systems in humanitarian, early recovery, and development contexts. The TA will focus on system‑based sanitation approaches, moving beyond isolated infrastructure to improved service chains from containment, emptying, transport, treatment, and safe disposal or reuse. Support will include technical guidance on context‑appropriate FSM models for urban and small‑town settings, integration of sanitation into cholera prevention and epidemic preparedness strategies, and development of sustainable operation and maintenance arrangements. The TA will also address climate and environmental considerations, including flood‑resilient sanitation, safe sludge treatment, and reduction of environmental contamination, thereby strengthening public health and environmental outcomes. Expected Outputs / Deliverables Technical guidance on sanitation and FSM service‑chain design Context‑appropriate sanitation and FSM models for fragile settings Strengthened integration of sanitation into cholera prevention programming Improved technical capacity of staff and partners on sanitation systems

desc: Technical assistance to strengthen climate‑resilient and standards‑compliant WASH in institutions, with a focus on World Bank‑aligned WASH in health facilities
full: This technical assistance will provide specialized support to strengthen the technical quality, climate resilience, and sustainability of WASH services in institutions, with a primary focus on health facilities and targeted support to schools and learning environments where relevant. The TA will emphasize system functionality, reliability, and long‑term operation and maintenance, rather than standalone infrastructure delivery. For health facilities, the assistance will focus on improving water supply reliability, sanitation and wastewater management, hygiene infrastructure, and waste management systems, ensuring alignment with international infection prevention and control (IPC) standards and World Bank Environmental and Social Standards (ESS). Particular attention will be given to climate‑resilient design, including water source resilience, backup systems, and adaptation to climate risks such as droughts and floods. The TA will support technical design review, development of practical guidance and standards, and strengthening of operation and maintenance (O&M) arrangements for institutional WASH. This support will help reduce implementation and compliance risks, particularly in the context of World Bank‑financed health sector operations, while improving sustainability and service continuity in fragile and climate‑stressed environments. Expected Outputs / Deliverables Technical guidance and review inputs for WASH in health facilities and schools Climate‑resilient design and O&M recommendations for institutional WASH systems Strengthened alignment with IPC standards and World Bank ESS requirements Improved technical capacity of staff and partners on institutional WASH quality assurance

desc: WASH Information Management, GIS & Digital Monitoring Systems
full: This technical assistance will support UNICEF Yemen to strengthen WASH information management systems, including the use of GIS, digital monitoring tools, and integrated data platforms to support evidence‑based planning, programme monitoring, and decision‑making. The TA will focus on improving data quality, interoperability, and practical use of WASH data across humanitarian and development programming. Support will include technical guidance on GIS‑based mapping of WASH infrastructure and services, development or refinement of digital monitoring frameworks, and integration of WASH data with climate risk, water resources, and health indicators where feasible. The assistance will also help strengthen capacity for routine data analysis, visualization, and use at national and sub‑national levels, ensuring that digital tools support programme quality, accountability, and adaptive management rather than parallel reporting systems. Expected Outputs / Deliverables GIS and digital monitoring guidance adapted to Yemen WASH context Improved WASH data frameworks and visualization tools Strengthened capacity of staff and partners on WASH information management Better integration of WASH data into planning and reporting processes

desc: Strengthen Rural Community‑Based WASH Management & Sustainability Models
full: This technical assistance will support UNICEF Yemen to strengthen community‑based WASH management models in rural areas, with a focus on sustainability, local ownership, and long‑term functionality of water and sanitation services. The TA will aim to move beyond short‑term community engagement toward structured, accountable, and technically sound management arrangements adapted to fragile and conflict‑affected contexts. Support will include technical guidance on governance and management models for rural water schemes, roles and responsibilities of community institutions, basic financial management and cost recovery options, operation and maintenance arrangements, and linkages with local authorities and service providers. The assistance will also integrate climate resilience and water resource sustainability considerations into community‑based management approaches. Expected Outputs / Deliverables Practical guidance on community‑based WASH management models Strengthened O&M and governance frameworks for rural WASH systems Integration of climate resilience into rural WASH management approaches Improved capacity of staff, partners, and communities

desc: UNICEF Armenia Country Office is keen to engage in the expansion of innovative learning programmes under UNICEF’s new global education strategy, particularly it
full: UNICEF Armenia Country Office's interest in exploring the opportunity to participate in the expansion of innovative learning programmes, announced as part of UNICEF's transformative global education strategy launched at Educa in Helsinki last week. I am particularly inspired by the Strategy's deliberate shifts toward putting teachers and learners at the center while prioritizing equity. The Government of Armenia recognizes the critical importance of EdTech to transform education delivery. Active discussions are currently underway at the Ministry of Education, Science, Culture and Sports (MoESCS) with relevant stakeholders regarding the role of EdTech and AI in education. While several pilot and innovative initiatives exist in both formal and informal education, a comprehensive framework and system-wide approach are currently missing—making this an opportune moment for UNICEF strategic intervention. Armenia presents a unique opportunity for scaling innovative learning programmes due to the strong government commitment to digital transformation and presence of companies delivering innovative solutions. In 2024, the MoESCS adopted new state standards for Digital Literacy and Computer Science (DLCS), aiming to equip students with practical, future-ready programming skills, computational thinking, and digital literacy. To ensure effective implementation of these standards, UNICEF, in collaboration with the Ministry and in partnership with the Foundation for Armenian Science and Technology (FAST), is supporting a pilot programme to capacitate DLCS teachers to deliver the new curriculum. We are simultaneously supporting the digitalization of teacher training courses through the integration of LMS. Participation in the global innovative learning programmes would enable Armenia to: Build upon existing initiatives with a comprehensive, system-wide approach Align national efforts with global best practices and evidence-based solutions Accelerate progress toward measurable learning outcomes with equity at the core Strengthen the capacity of teachers through innovative tools and methodologies I would greatly appreciate the opportunity to discuss Armenia's potential participation in the initial phase or subsequent phases of the Strategy's rollout. A meeting would allow us to: Explore specific programme alignment with Armenia's education priorities Discuss implementation modalities and timelines Identify partnership opportunities and resource requirements Determine next steps for formal engagement

desc: Request to reinstate the Learning Passport (LP) platform in Mozambique, following its shutdown last November due to inactivity.
full: UNICEF Mozambique has reassessed the situation and successfully re-engaged the Ministry of Education, renewing interest in leveraging technology to transform the education system. The urgency is clear: Mozambique faces significant challenges in ensuring learning continuity. Over two million children remain out of school, dropout rates are high and learning outcomes for those enrolled are alarmingly low. The education system is overstretched and underfunded, and the outlook is further complicated by rapid population growth, economic stagnation, ongoing conflict, and the impacts of climate change. To reverse this downward trend, a bold transformation of the education sector is needed—one that harnesses the power of technology to expand access, improve quality, and build resilience. In close coordination with the Ministry of Education, UNICEF Mozambique is committed to reviving the Learning Passport with a clear and strategic vision and building on lessons learned from previous efforts: • To deliver curriculum-aligned content to children both in and out of school • To build foundational and 21st-century skills • To strengthen teacher capacity through digital professional development modules

desc: Supporting successful curriculum reform and strengthening learning outcomes
full: Sri Lanka begins rolling out its new curriculum in Grades 1 and 6 in 2026, alongside a national learning assessment. This reform has the potential to modernise teaching and restore learning trajectories after years of disruption, but challenges remain. One key challenge is not the design of the curriculum but its acceptance—by teachers accustomed to tuition-driven, exam-focused practices, and by communities that may be wary of pedagogical change. The priority for 2026 is to ensure the reform succeeds by helping identify bottlenecks early, monitoring classroom realities, and supporting strategies that build teacher and community confidence in the new approach. As details of implementation become clearer in Q1, UNICEF will refine the support package, with particular attention to child-centered pedagogy and development of a teacher professional development framework, strengthening monitoring and mentoring mechanisms, education behaviour change, communication, and practical tools that help teachers make the shift in pedagogy but support to ensure a successful reform journey for Sri Lanka is required.

desc: Domestic Financing and Immunization Sustainability Strategy Support for Malawi
full: Malawi’s primary health care system faces persistent financing challenges, with declining prioritization of immunisation and essential PHC services threatening service continuity and sustainability. Despite the Government’s commitment to Universal Health Coverage, budget allocations and execution for immunisation remain constrained by competing fiscal pressures, foreign exchange volatility, and limited medium-term expenditure planning. Strengthening domestic financing for PHC is critical to safeguard essential services and ensure sustainable vaccine delivery in line with HSSP III and the Lusaka Agenda.To address these challenges, UNICEF Malawi requests technical assistance to strengthen domestic financing for PHC, with a focus on reversing the declining prioritization of immunisation financing. The support will build on ongoing CO budget analysis work, translating fiscal evidence into actionable analytics and policy tools to influence Government of Malawi, Ministry of Health, and Treasury investment decisions. It will consolidate and deepen current PHC and immunisation financing analyses through a rapid diagnostic integrating budget trends, execution performance, and immunisation sustainability modelling. The TA will generate forward-looking scenarios for vaccine co-financing under varying macroeconomic conditions, assess delivery cost bottlenecks and value-for-money opportunities, and identify practical efficiency and reprioritization levers. Additionally, it will support the development of a budget protection framework for vaccines and essential PHC services, including earmarking and contingency financing options, medium-term expenditure projections, and concrete policy measures to strengthen immunisation prioritization within MoH budgets and the national Medium-Term Expenditure Framework.

desc: HPV Plus Strategy and Differentiated Vaccination Support for Adolescents Living with HIV (ALHIV)
full: Zimbabwe is implementing the HPV Plus initiative under its National HPV Revitalization Strategy, approved in February 2025, which aims to raise HPV vaccination coverage to 90% by 2030. The strategy aligns with WHO guidance by introducing a differentiated schedule for adolescents living with HIV (ALHIV), who require two doses instead of the single dose given to the general population. Despite this progress, major gaps persist in reaching ALHIV, who face a higher risk of persistent HPV infection and cervical cancer. Coverage remains particularly low among out‑of‑school adolescents and those from marginalized groups. Weak integration between HIV care services and HPV vaccination programs leads to missed opportunities to identify ALHIV and ensure completion of the two‑dose schedule. In addition, many healthcare providers lack sufficient training to deliver differentiated HPV services and tailored counselling. These challenges are further compounded by poorly integrated HIV and HPV data systems, limiting effective tracking of vaccination status and follow‑up for second doses. To operationalize the HPV Plus initiative for adolescents living with HIV (ALHIV), Zimbabwe requires targeted technical assistance to strengthen differentiated HPV vaccination delivery. Priority needs include developing standardized operational guidance and user‑friendly job aids to support implementation of the two‑dose schedule, and identifying effective service delivery platforms informed by best practices from countries with successful ALHIV HPV vaccination programs.

desc: Community Feedback, Social Accountability and Immunization Demand Strengthening Support
full: Malawi continues to face challenges related to zero-dose and missed children. Reaching zero-dose children and missed children requires an integrated primary health care (PHC) approach that address gender-related barriers, social norms, and structural barriers, while building resilient and sustained demand for immunisation services. Improved health outcomes depend on empowered communities and strengthened social accountability mechanisms that actively engage communities in participatory planning, implementation, and monitoring of health services. Building and sustaining trust in immunisation services is therefore essential and requires timely, coordinated, and evidence-based responses to community voices, concerns and satisfaction. Malawi Country Office has been collecting community feedback, rumours, and misinformation through multiple channels—both online (e.g. U-Report, media monitoring) and offline (surveys, rapid qualitative assessments, and field monitoring) but these data remain fragmented. Information is stored across different platforms and its lacks national feedback system which consolidate, analyse, and act on community insights.There is a critical need to establish one community feedback and response mechanism that integrates data from all existing platforms. This system will be able to do real-time analysis, coordinated response planning, and systematic use of community feedback to inform programme adjustments and policy decisions. This mechanism will support evidence-based decision-making, improve responsiveness to community concerns and rumours, and ultimately strengthen demand for immunisation and other essential health services.

desc: SBC Capacity Assessment and Curriculum Development Support
full: There is growing recognition within Viet Nam’s Ministry of Health (MOH) and other line ministries of the need for more comprehensive, system-oriented SBC strategies. However, institutional capacity for SBC research, design, implementation, and monitoring remains limited. With increasing digital connectivity, there is also a need to better integrate behavioral insights and digital engagement to enhance inclusion, equity, and sustainability. Strengthening SBC across sectors will support more effective health and social interventions, greater community participation, and sustainable behavior change at scale. To address this, UNICEF Viet Nam, in collaboration with MOH, is conducting a rapid organizational and capacity assessment of SBC programmes, with a focus on immunization. The assessment will identify key barriers to scale and existing capacities within the health system. Based on the findings, UNICEF will support the development of an SBC curriculum to strengthen MOH staff capacity in planning, budgeting, managing, and monitoring SBC programmes. UNICEF Viet Nam is seeking TA support to provide technical review, inputs, and guidance to ensure the quality of both the assessment and the curriculum development.

desc: MNH Best Practices Identification & Quality Improvement Support (Perinatal Mortality Reduction)
full: After several engagements, we identified Ecuador as one of the countries that is implementing an interesting approach to integrated Quality Improvement interventions for MNCH with support from UNICEF Ecuador Country Office. The Ecuador Country Office facilitated engagements with their MOH counterparts, implementing partners and academic institution. On the 9th of June, the COE organized a virtual meeting among MOH programe leads from MOH of Ecuador and Costa Rica, UNICEF colleagues from Argentina, Costa Rica and Ecuador and facilitated by the COE. Detailed presentations were made and which lead to robust discussions. Some of the key lessons learned were: 1. MNCH Quality improvement interventions require a systematic approach based on data and evidence 2. A robust system for monitoring, documentation and knowledge management was critical for success. 3. It's important to identify highly successful interventions and refine them for scale up. Even though this TA was requested by Argentina, the COE identified Costa Rica as a country that could benefit from this south to south exchange and invited Costa Rica to join the meeting and this was very useful for the MOH and the Social Security Fund of Costa Rica. Next steps: 1. Ecuador Country Office, MOH, and the implementing partners will share the intervention tools to participants. 2. Both Argentina and Costa Rica expressed strong interest to learn from countries that are implementing neonatal near miss case reviews/audits. Therefore, teh COE will organize a second learning session on neonatal near miss review.

desc: Phasing Out Face-to-Face MNCH Training through a Sustainable Capacity Development System
full: UNICEF has invested significantly in strengthening the competencies of healthcare providers and community health workers in MNCH, largely through recurrent face-to-face training. While these efforts have strengthened knowledge and skills, they require substantial financial and human resources and are difficult to sustain and scale, particularly for workers in remote areas. The absence of a systematic monitoring mechanism also limits assessment of learning, competency development and application of skills in practice. UNICEF will therefore support the Ministry of Health through 2028 to progressively phase out UNICEF-supported face-to-face training and establish a sustainable, government-owned system for continuous learning and competency development. This will include institutionalizing digital learning, simulation, telemedicine and virtual mentoring, partnerships with universities and training institutions, and, as needed, accreditation and continuing education credit systems. A monitoring system will track learning and application of skills. From 2029, the system will be led and sustained by the Government.

desc: Community Health Workforce Professionalisation and Career Pathway Development Support
full: Malawi’s community health workforce including HSAs, CHNs, and CHVs forms the backbone of primary health care delivery, particularly at the community level. Despite their critical role, the workforce faces fragmented career pathways, limited progression opportunities, and inconsistent integration into formal health structures. Strengthening the professionalisation of this cadre is essential to improve motivation, retention, and quality of service delivery, in line with HSSP III, the National Community Health Framework, and broader HRH reforms.To address these gaps, UNICEF Malawi requests technical assistance to professionalise the community health workforce, with a primary focus on designing clear career progression pathways. The support will define competency standards, accreditation, and progression for all community cadres, integrate them into formal PHC structures with appropriate supervision and retention mechanisms, ensure alignment with district operational plans and national HRH systems, and provide guidance for institutionalisation and sustainable workforce management to strengthen PHC delivery and advance Universal Health Coverage.

desc: Resilient PHC Systems and Emergency Preparedness Support
full: Malawi’s primary health care system is increasingly exposed to multiple emergency hazards, including climate shocks, disease outbreaks, and other public health threats, which threaten service continuity and resilience. Despite progress in PHC coverage, emergency events can rapidly disrupt essential services, particularly for vulnerable populations. Strengthening system resilience and maintaining or increasing PHC intervention coverage requires strategic approaches that integrate preparedness, adaptive service delivery, and coordinated response mechanisms, in line with HSSP III and broader health sector reforms.To address these challenges, UNICEF Malawi requests technical assistance to support the strategic design and implementation of PHC interventions that maintain and expand coverage while enhancing system resilience. The support will focus on adaptive service delivery models, strategic prepositioning of essential supplies and resources, and the development of expanded multi-stakeholder partnerships to ensure continuity of services during emergencies. The TA will provide guidance on operationalising emergency preparedness and response plans within routine PHC delivery, identifying system bottlenecks, optimizing resource allocation, and integrating lessons from previous hazard responses to strengthen both short-term emergency response and long-term system resilience.Expected outputs include a strategic framework for resilient PHC delivery under emergency conditions, operational guidance for adaptive service delivery, prepositioning plans for essential supplies, and partnership strategies to support sustainable emergency response and continuity of essential PHC services.

desc: Shift Eritrea’s food systems from production-focused approaches to nutrition outcomes through integrated value chains, schools, food safety, and SBC
full: Module A — Rapid food systems mapping & priority entry points (≈ 8 weeks) What CoE does: Produce a concise map of nutrition-sensitive value chains (e.g., cereals/legumes, dairy) and school-based entry points (gardens/menus), with a baseline of risks and simple indicators. Identify quick wins in food safety and hygiene practices across small processors/school kitchens; map governance and cross-ministry roles (MoA/MoH/MoE/MLWE). What it strengthens: Shared picture of “where to start” linking production to nutrition outcomes; early list of feasible pilots; clarity on roles and decision points. Standards/tools: UNICEF food systems/nutrition guidance; simple value-chain and risk screening templates; school nutrition checklist. Module B — Complementary foods mini-pilot (DMK+) & micro-processing support What CoE does: Co-design a small DMK+ complementary food mini-pilot: product specifications, quality/batch SOPs, basic HACCP-inspired hygiene steps, packaging/labelling, and micro-processing coaching for 2–3 local producer units (or school kitchens). Develop simple QA tools and a child-feeding counselling card that links to the product. What it strengthens: Safe, acceptable complementary foods with clear quality steps; local capacity to produce and coach caregivers; documented micro-processing SOPs for replication. Standards/tools: UNICEF IYCF resources; QA/food safety lite templates; behaviour change job-aids. Module C — Food safety & fortification “lite”: SOPs and training What CoE does: Draft light SOPs for hygiene, storage, and fortification/processing suitable for small establishments and schools; run two short training cycles (virtual + in-country practical sessions) for MoH/MoA/MoE/MMR/MTI teams and local producers. Provide model procurement specs (e.g., packaging, basic test kits) and simple monitoring forms. What it strengthens: Practical, context-appropriate standards that reduce contamination and variability; entry-level capacity to monitor compliance. Standards/tools: Food safety checklists; school kitchen hygiene SOP; fortification basics; simple monitoring templates. Module D — Healthy diets SBC & school-based pilots (gardens/menus/peer clubs) What CoE does: Package an SBC toolkit (scripts/posters/mini-sessions) on diverse diets and safe food handling; set up 10–15 school garden/menu/peer clubs pilots with seasonally feasible crops and a simple menu planning sheet; define a light results log (attendance, menu diversity, hygiene practices). What it strengthens: Community and school behaviours for healthier diets; practical experience with school gardens and simple menu standards; early evidence for scale-up. Standards/tools: SBC toolkit; garden starter kit; menu diversity scorecard; hygiene reminders.

desc: Prevent post-cyclone nutrition and food security crises through anticipatory, child-focused action

Both wasting and stunting rates were concerning prior to the cyclone, and we expect additional shocks to push vulnerable households into deeper food stress. Our priority for 2026 is to position UNICEF to lead the development of a coherent package of short-term and medium-term interventions—ranging from targeted nutrition support and continuity of essential services to systems-level measures that strengthen surveillance, early warning, and household resilience. Sri Lanka will have limited fiscal space next year (and the CO will have limited funding) but the need for clear analysis, costed options, and strong advocacy remains urgent. UNICEF will need to identify feasible entry points and shaping an integrated proposal/clear advocacy that government and partners can get behind, rollout and budget for in subsequent years.

desc: Yemen is conducting Groundwater potential mapping and would like oversight support and insights from lessons learnt in other countries
full: The Minister of Water has requested UNICEF to develop an Integrated Watershed Management Plan for Taizz City. This task was broken down into 3 studies (i) a remote sending study to develop a groundwater potential map, (ii) an emergency well field and water supply infrastructure study, and (iii) the development of an Integrated Watershed Management Plan, building on the first 2 studies. Under the UNICEF ToR for the Remote Sensing study, the primary scope was focused on remote sensing–based groundwater potential mapping. In a first step Acacia Water conducted a data gap analysis, including: (i) a clear overview of datasets to be used, (ii) verification of required data availability and quality, (iii) a structured data gap analysis, and (iv) recommendation for the way forward, was conducted through an existing standby agreement mechanism. The intention was to keep the assignment of the actual Remote Sensing study targeted, realistic and cost-efficient, with additional analytical layers potentially integrated in the actual Remote Sensing study. The Ministry of Water has since proposed expanding the scope of the Remote Sensing study to include additional components: agricultural water demand assessment, surface runoff evaluation, land-use analysis and its impact on water use, climate change considerations, incorporation of existing groundwater monitoring data, and integration of water quality datasets. Given this expanded scope, we request: (1) an indication on associated costs for expanded scope; (2) Support with the technical evaluation of the proposals expected by the end of March, (3) sharing lessons learned and cost benchmarks from similar groundwater mapping initiatives in other country contexts to inform decision-making (4) Oversight support during implementation.

full: UNICEF Somalia will roll out its Nadiif Integrated Model for rural sanitation starting pilot interventions in selected districts. The Model proposes three interconnected pillars on strengthening government leadership, an enhanced approach to CLTS and harnessing the private sector. Lack of government oversight on sanitation and in-access to supplies have been a major constraint. As part of institutional preparation and readiness for this roll out, UNICEF is supporting the government to put in place statutory instruments to guide this effort. desc: Support development of a national WASH Financing Strategy for Somalia.
full: Somalia is one of the ASWA III countries. Under this programme, the Dutch government prioritized a few thematic areas including WASH financing. UNICEF Somalia is undertaking analysis in this area to obtain data and information to inform development of a WASH Financing Strategy. The aim is to develop a holistic WASH Sector Financing Strategy that aligns with Somalia’s WASH national policy commitments, National Transformation Plan and/or Sustainable Development Goal 6 (SDG 6) aspirations. For this, UNICEF Somalia requests technical support from refining data collection tools to review of the report/ findings and the development of a WASH Financing Strategy.

desc: ASWA: Support towards Gender Landscape Analysis in Puntland and Somaliland.
full: Under ASWA III, the request is for technical support to conduct a gender landscape analysis in Somalia. The analysis aims to identify gender related gaps, power dynamics, inequalities, barriers, opportunities, and systemic issues affecting WASH access, governance, participation, and outcomes. It will generate practical, evidence based recommendations and tools to strengthen gender transformative and inclusive WASH programming across the programme cycle. The required support will include technical inputs throughout the gender landscape analysis process, including preparatory activities such as partner capacity building and training prior to data collection, review of the draft report following completion of the analysis, development of an action and response plan, and preparation of training and capacity building materials.

desc: Support development and review of climate rationales for Somaliland and Puntland.
full: Development of a climate rationale is one of the key priorities under ASWA III. The process is already underway in both states, with Somaliland having completed the climate risk analysis and solutions workshop to identify feasible measures to address the identified risks. The climate rationales will support: • Policy and planning processes • Design and targeting of climate resilient WASH programmes • Development of climate finance proposals, including for the Green Climate Fund • Improved alignment between WASH and climate priorities, including Somalia’s updated Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) and the National Adaptation Plan (NAP) The required support includes technical review of the climate risk and solutions reports generated through these processes, as well as review of the final Climate Rationale products for Somaliland and Puntland.

desc: 【UTS】Life-cycle costing for climate-resilient rural sanitation (3 provinces)
full: Apply a life-cycle costing approach to estimate the full cost of moving rural households from open defecation to basic sanitation and to climate-resilient sanitation across three provinces. The work combines data analysis with statistical/spatial methods to extrapolate costs at provincial level, building on existing data and design efforts for the Government’s No Open Defecation (NOD) programme. Outputs are being shaped through stakeholder engagement, including a government/stakeholder workshop held in Honiara (24 March 2026) and dissemination moments such as sector events

desc: 【UTS】NbS monitoring system for water availability & resilience
full: Design a monitoring approach (indicators, tools, and methods) to assess how nature-based water conservation interventions contribute to water availability and selected dimensions of community resilience. The approach builds on the regional resilience monitoring guidance and is intended for piloting and potential adoption within wider sector monitoring led by DNRAS and partners, including UNICEF’s collaboration with Permatil. Progress includes agreement on the monitoring approach, training delivered with Permatil, researchers recruited for the community-resilience component, and field equipment delivered (loggers/flow-measurement tools).

desc: 【UTS】Coastal salinity testing & analysis for climate response
full: Support salinity monitoring in selected coastal locations through government-led surveys and technical review, focusing on conductivity and TDS indicators to identify potential salinity intrusion risks. Initial surveys in three locations were conducted and reviewed, indicating salinity did not appear excessive in those sites; next steps include UNICEF-led quality assurance/validation and additional technical review by UTS to confirm findings and determine whether further testing is warranted

desc: 【UTS】Assess septic tanks’ impact on groundwater quality (safely managed sanitation) in Kiritimati
full: Conduct a longitudinal assessment of shallow groundwater quality around newly installed septic tanks to understand potential contamination pathways and impacts. Work completed includes agreement on study design, government buy-in, construction of 40 piezometers across 5 sites (households and one school), installation of rain gauges and water level loggers, and soil sampling; groundwater sampling is scheduled to begin late March/early April. A final report will synthesise findings and implications for safely managed sanitation

desc: 【UTS】Lao PDR technical support package (WSP, GEDSI, LCC, private sector)
full: Deliver a multi-part technical assistance package: (1) develop climate-resilient water safety planning (WSP) guidelines incorporating GEDSI perspectives; (2) assess life-cycle costs of community-managed water services and develop tools/workshops for government use; (3) scope private sector service delivery models and investment/business case through literature review and interviews (e.g., SNV, Gret, Thrive, TerraClear); and (4) provide ongoing GEDSI oversight/support to ensure inclusion is embedded in planning processes. Current progress includes financial analysis reporting shared for review and private sector interviews completed, with final outputs being prepared for sharing.

desc: Selection of Food Technologist to Support Pillar 1 of Tanzania's FFA
full: Support the selection process of the following individual consultancy process: Food Technologist (Complementary Foods) – National Individual Consultant Scope of Work: The purpose of this consultancy is to support the development, validation, and scale-up of affordable, safe, and nutrient-dense complementary food products for children aged 6–23 months in Tanzania. Key Tasks • Conduct landscape analysis and stakeholder engagement by reviewing existing complementary food products, supply chains, and regulatory frameworks, mapping key actors (e.g. manufacturers, laboratories, ingredient suppliers, distributors, government agencies, NGOs and academia institutions), and defining product profiles in consultation with stakeholders. With special focus in prioritized regions: Dar es Salaam, Arusha, Mbeya, Mwanza and Zanzibar. • Support the validation of the mapping report and database creation of local food producers. • Support with key partners product research, development, and validation by formulating and optimizing at least two nutrient-dense complementary food products using locally available ingredients. This includes ensuring adequate nutrient density, protein quality, micronutrient bioavailability (e.g. iron, zinc) energy density, safety, and sensory acceptability; defining processing and packaging parameters (e.g. extrusion, roasting, germination), packaging specifications and critical control points; and overseeing laboratory testing and refinement through accredited labs and refine formulations accordingly. • Strengthen food safety, quality assurance, and regulatory compliance systems by supporting the development and implementation of training toolkits (including HACCP, GMP, and SSOP protocols); support building capacity of producers and quality assurance teams through targeted training; developing compliant product labeling in line with national regulations and the International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes; and establishing shelf-life testing protocols as well as market surveillance and monitoring mechanisms. • Support local producers and SMEs through continuous, hands-on technical assistance to improve production processes of nutritious first foods, ensure food safety and quality standards are met, and facilitate reformulation of existing products to meet national and international standards. • In collaboration with key partners support the development of business and distribution models by designing costed, sustainable approaches for production and last-mile delivery; identifying risks and mitigation strategies; and exploring market feasibility of the developed products, based on evidence generated. • Support the development of technical tools and strengthen capacity among governments, producers, SMEs, and partners through training materials, standard operating procedures (SOPs), workshops, webinars, and on-site coaching, promoting long-term sustainability using the training toolkit developed by UNICEF. • Facilitate knowledge sharing and coordination by establishing and maintaining a network of local farmers, processors, and stakeholders to promote quality assurance, innovation, and continuous learning, while ensuring regular coordination with UNICEF and partners. • Support the generation and dissemination of evidence on product acceptability, shelf-life, and market potential, and compile a final report summarizing key findings, achievements, challenges, and recommendations for scale-up. • Support other activities agreed as relevant to the objectives of the consultancy.

desc: Review Sudan Tariff study ToR
full: In support to the UNICEF Sudan team in reviewing and implementing the Urban Water Supply Tariff Review, the following is proposed: Assessment of the ToRs (i) Relevance in the Sudanese Context The Sudanese urban water sector is currently defined by structural underfinancing, where regional utilities are heavily subsidized and the Ministry of Finance typically covers staff salaries while internal revenues fail to meet even basic O&M costs. Metered billing is largely not practiced, with most systems relying on flat-rate monthly fees that do not reflect actual usage, contributing to high Non-Revenue Water (NRW) levels estimated at 40%. Furthermore, current revenue collection is often tied to the Electricity Company (EC), which charges a 13% commission and creates a disconnect between the utility and its customers. In this environment, water management is often driven by a political agenda rather than commercial logic, treating water as a service rather than a commodity.
