desc: Support to Angola CO on several PFM-related work areas
full: Title: Strengthening Capacity for Public Expenditure Reviews (PER) and Budget Transparency in Angola Short Description of Request UNICEF Angola, in collaboration with the Ministry of Finance (MINFIN), seeks technical assistance from the Centre of Excellence (CoE) to strengthen national capacity to conduct Public Expenditure Reviews (PERs), with a focus on health and education sectors, and to enhance budget transparency practices. The request will support the development of a practical, step-by-step PER manual tailored to Angola, complemented by capacity building and in-country training for MINFIN and key stakeholders. The support will also incorporate innovative approaches, including the use of AI tools, to improve efficiency and analytical quality in PER processes. Objectives Overall Objective To build sustainable national capacity within MINFIN and partner institutions to independently design and implement high-quality Public Expenditure Reviews and improve evidence-based budgeting. Specific Objectives Develop a PER Methodological Manual Produce a practical, step-by-step guide tailored to Angola’s institutional and fiscal context Include core PER methodology and simplified modules for sector-specific analysis (health and education) Integrate guidance on the use of digital and AI tools for data analysis, forecasting, and reporting Strengthen Institutional Capacity Train MINFIN, MINPLAN, and selected sector ministries on PER concepts, methodology, and application Build a core national team capable of leading PER processes Promote Standardization and Sustainability Establish a consistent framework and tools for future PERs across sectors Institutionalize PER practices within government systems Enhance Analytical Tools and Innovation Introduce practical guidance on leveraging AI and data tools (e.g., for expenditure analysis, data cleaning, trend analysis, visualization) Encourage efficient use of existing administrative and financial data systems Expected Support from CoE The CoE would provide both technical expertise and capacity-building support , including: 1. Development of PER Manual Review existing PER work in Angola (e.g., Health PER 2022, other sectoral reviews) Develop a structured manual including: PER concepts, purpose, and typologies Step-by-step methodology (planning, data collection, analysis, reporting) Public finance diagnostic tools Expenditure efficiency and equity analysis Institutional and governance analysis Sector-specific annexes (health and education) Templates, checklists, and sample outputs Section on use of AI tools and digital solutions (e.g., for data processing, visualization, benchmarking) 2. Capacity Building and Training Design and deliver training workshops (in-country, Angola) Target participants: MINFIN (core focus) MINPLAN Selected sector ministries (Health, Education) Training to cover: PER methodology Hands-on use of tools/templates Practical exercises using Angola data (if feasible) Introduction to AI-supported analytics 3. Coaching and Technical Backstopping Provide follow-up support (remote) Support application of the manual in a pilot/practical setting (if feasible) Expected Deliverables Inception Report (to be done mostly by ACO, with inputs from CoE) Workplan, methodology, and structure of the PER manual Mapping of existing PERs and relevant diagnostics in Angola PER Manual (Angola-tailored) Comprehensive but practical guide Includes: Core methodology Sector-specific modules (health & education) Tools/templates AI integration guidance Training Package Training materials (presentations, case studies, exercises) Participant handbook In-country Training Delivery At least one multi-day workshop delivered in Luanda Training report with key outcomes and recommendations AI Tools Guidance Note (Standalone or integrated) Practical, user-friendly note on applying AI tools in PER Final Report Summary of activities, results, and recommendations for institutionalizing PER practice in Angola Key Expectations from CoE Provide hands-on, implementation-oriented expertise (not purely theoretical) Draw on international good practices while tailoring to Angola’s context Ensure outputs are practical, usable, and owned by MINFIN Incorporate innovative approaches, including AI and data tools, in a realistic and accessible manner Deliver capacity-building that creates long-term institutional capability Suggested Timeline (Indicative) Month 1 (June 2026): Inception and review of existing materials Months 2–3 (July and August 2026): Draft PER manual Month 4-5 (September and October 2026): Training preparation and in-country training delivery Month 6 (November 2026): Finalization and reporting Strategic Relevance This TA directly contributes to: Strengthening public finance management systems Improving social sector expenditure efficiency Advancing budget transparency and accountability (including Open Budget indicators)

desc: Digitalization of child health records
full: UNICEF Djibouti is seeking technical assistance to support the scale-up of the digitalization of child health records across integrated management of childhood illness (IMCI), integrated community case management (iCCM), and the electronic vaccination card. Djibouti has already started piloting the digitalization of IMCI folder records in six health facilities using the DHIS2 platform. The support is expected to help define a scalable, interoperable, and user-centred approach that strengthens continuity of care across community and facility levels, improves child-level follow-up, and enhances timely identification and management of missed, sick, under-immunized, and vulnerable children. The assistance should align with national digital health architecture and support integrated service delivery across primary health care, nutrition, and immunization platforms.

desc: Pilot of the Public Procurement Efficiency priogramme in Sierra Leone within the Education Sector
full: Work with the Ministry of Basic and Senor Secondary Education, the Ministry of Technical and Higher Education and Ministry of Finance on the following Steps, Key Activities and Analysis: 1. Develop a Value for Money Agenda Agree with MBSSE/MTHE and MoF on priority commodities and processes to target (e.g. textbooks, furniture, school supplies). Review existing policies; set monitoring indicators and implementation structures; produce a workplan and agreed terms of reference. 2. Identify Inefficiencies Full diagnostic of the procurement cycle: map actors, resource flows, rules and decision points. Identify bottlenecks – misaligned budget and procurement timelines, fragmented systems, weak specifications, payment arrears, limited competition, etc. Produce a prioritised action plan. 3. Monitor and Measure Savings Assess existing M&E and IFMIS capacity to track savings at each procurement stage. Strengthen data collection and reporting. Institutionalise routine VfM analysis – comparing contracted prices to benchmarks, tracking budget execution against procurement plans. 4. Protect and Reinvest via PFM Diagnose the PFM rules governing what happens to savings (annuality, rollover, common pooling rules). Identify options ranging from in-year reprioritisation within MBSSE/MTHE to creation of protected budget lines and MTEF embedding. Advocate for legal or administrative changes where needed.

Reform Acceleration and Technical Advice Provide technical advice on gender-responsive, disability-inclusive and needs-based social protection reforms, including service delivery systems, disability inclusion, service coordination mechanisms and social welfare reform priorities. 2. Reform Scoping and Activity Prioritization Support development of detailed implementation pathways, activity prioritization and sequencing for GRSP II activities and Government reform priorities, including identification of operational bottlenecks and technical support needs. 3. Data Systems and Service Integration Provide technical inputs on strengthening social protection information systems, data exchange mechanisms, interoperability opportunities and service integration approaches within existing platforms and institutional arrangements. 5. desc: Support on light version of Sustainability Checks
full: Time has flowed under the bridge since we exchanged last February, but I did not stay inactive and might propose you an approach to strongly position UNICEF in WASH at upstream level in Argentina that fits to the objectives set in the CPD. Reading the CPD and the priorities in the Child health and nutrition Section, I understand that UNICEF ACO’s priorities are articulated around advocacy action to provide support to the (provincial) government(s) to design and implement of evidence-based local policies, plans and programmes, strengthen cross-sectoral programmes and support institutional capacity to improve the quality and coverage of services. In some municipalities of Chaco, Formosa, Santiago del Estero and in urban slums, there are structural stunting area (with very low municipal revenue per capita, high reliance on transfers, rural and peri-urban poverty) where stunting ranges from 15% to 20% (similar rates as Ghana, Kenya or Senegal). In these contexts, unsustainable WASH services are a key structural driver of inequity and child undernutrition. Reading the article attached in my message (focusing on the sustainability of water services in the Province of Santa Fe, which I do imagine has similar challenges than the other Provinces), sustainability is critical and is associated to weak institutional capacity and governance, aging or inadequate infrastructure, financial constraints, insufficient participation of stakeholders, etc. If you are interested UNICEF ACO could implement a simplified Sector Wide Sustainability Check exercise (see: https://www.unicef.org/documents/unicef-sector-wide-sustainability-check-tool ) in cooperation with a Provincial Government (given the current context, I trust it would bear stronger fruits than implementing this exercise at national level). Such an exercise could aim to : Identify systemic bottlenecks (policy, governance, financing, capacity, service delivery, data) that undermine sustainability and equity. Distinguish infrastructure gaps from system failures, focusing on why services do not last or reach the most vulnerable. Inform strategic, upstream action, guiding UNICEF and governments toward system strengthening rather than isolated investments. Reduce sustainability risks to achieving SDG 6 and related child outcomes (nutrition, health, education). Support evidence ‑ based policy dialogue and prioritization, aligned with country programmes and national development plans. It could be the starting point for engaging a structured dialogue with key stakeholders and advocate for the UNICEF agenda (equity, climate resilience…) based on evidences. If you are interested : We could support the implementation of a simplified SWSC exercise. We have the opportunity this year to use a EU Grant and work with our partner IRCWASH, a Dutch-based think tank well known in the sector and with which we have a PCA (see: https://www.ircwash.org/ ) ; We could engage (through IRC, provided IRC would agree) a national consultant to land this exercise into the Argentinian reality. I have identified a potential consultant who is working with IDB on one hand and with WHO and UNICEF on the other hand on the GLAAS reports and WASH Accounts . See his CV attached; Once the SWSC exercise is completed, we could identify priority areas for UNICEF to engage and use Global Thematic Funds. Knowing the UNCIEF CO has low capacity in WASH, we could work with our partner iVL with which we also have a PCA (see: https://www.ivl.se/english/ivl/our-offer/international/wash.html ) to support a limited number of activities. iVL has a regional office in Bogota and has carried out already one mission in Argentina for LACRO. In parallel, UNICEF LACRO has a consultancy with an Spanish Speaker consultant to support the implementation of serval activities to improve Governments to strengthen national strategies to mainstream WASH and IPC in healthcare facilities (based on the joint WHO / UNICEF WASHFIT approach ). We potentially could synergize and designate Argentina as one of the targeted country (to be confirmed). A phased approach would consist in : Phase 1: implementing the SWSC exercise, review the results and identify the priority areas of work with the partners (up to October) ; Phase 2 (that can be developed in parallel of phase 1): support the WASH and IPC in healthcare facilities (with a possible visit of the consultant in September / October) ; Phase 3 : engage with IVL to define in more details UNICEF priorities in WASH for the 2026-2029 cycle. The first step would be to (i) explore if there is appetite to implement such an exercise and identify the province where the SWSC could be carried out (unless you would prefer a nationally-based exercise), (ii) place a request to UNICEF CoE, (iii) develop ToRs and engage with IRC. Please let me know if you want to discuss this further. I remain available.

desc: “Technical support for MENARO-led regional nutrition consultation with 12 MENA countries and partners to accelerate financing scale-up of nutrition actions.”
full: UNICEF MENARO, together with the Nutrition CoE Satellite team in Amman and in close coordination with the World Bank, to lead consultation that will bring together invited delegations, including government representatives, and technical teams from UNICEF and the World Bank, from across MENA countries. Key regional partners in nutrition, donors, academia, and civil society representatives will participate. 12 countries will be invited from the four MENA nutrition programming country clusters (per the MENA Nutrition Strategic Direction 2030): Djibouti, Egypt, Lebanon, Libya, Morocco, Oman, Saudi Arabia, State of Palestine, Sudan, Syria, Tunisia and Yemen. All these countries that have demonstrated progress in scaling up nutrition actions across diverse contexts, including countries with active World Bank investments and those with domestic investments/financing for nutrition (including countries with active Nutrition for Growth Commitments).

This work advances the CAAC, EVAC, and children on the move agendas across complex conflict contexts in MENA. It builds on consensus-building achieved with regional stakeholders on violence against children and harmful practices. It includes (1) implementing a strategic engagement plan for the Shattered Childhoods report, in support of MENARO advocacy and partnerships teams; (2) targeted engagement with Gulf donors to promote alternative care solutions for CAAC children; (3) sustained stakeholder engagement around third-country nationals in North-East Syria, supporting coordinated dialogue and protection-oriented responses; (4) Sustained technical engagement on multi-year plan agreed during Regional Ministerial Meeting on EVAC with the League of Arab States;(5) address emerging protection risks, including online violence against children; (6) technical assistance is required to support engagement with regional partners and donors to strengthen sustainable and domestically financed child protection systems. Sustained year on year engagement in updating the "shattered Childhoods" report and supporting the Implementation of engagement MENARO advocacy and partnerships team Implementation of the engagement plans on alternative care for children in situations of armed conflict with Gulf Area donors Sustained engagement with stakeholders in connection with TCN in Northeast Syria Progress on a multi-year plan agreed during Regional Ministerial Meeting to End Violence Against Children (EVAC) in partnership with the League of Arab States, including country-level commitments. Increased political commitment and policy dialogue with governments and regional partners to strengthen domestic financing for children, reflected in greater integration of child-focused priorities within national budget frameworks, public finance discussions, and national development plans. Regional advocacy and partnership initiatives launched to address online violence against children, including engagement with governments, regional organizations, and technology stakeholders. Technical assistance is needed to support the provision and interpretation of cross-sectoral data and analysis—particularly in health, nutrition, and child protection—during emergencies and key regional moments. This is especially important when major analytical products are released (e.g., IPC analyses for contexts such as Gaza) or when developing advocacy materials that require strong technical grounding such as providing data and informatoin on the impact of the current military escalation in the region on education. Support is also required to contextualize global products for the regional level, an important step in positioning UNICEF on critical programmatic issues. This has been a priority for the RO and done multiple times in recent years across sectors including health, education, and nutrition.

desc: MOPH has mandated immediate electronic prescription rollout across Afghan health facilities
full: UNICEF Afghanistan Country Office (ACO) is seeking technical assistance to support the Ministry of Public Health (MoPH) in response to a recent directive on the introduction of electronic prescription practices across selected health facilities. The request stems from ongoing discussions between UNICEF and MoPH, where there is a need to better understand how to approach the digitization of prescription processes in a structured, scalable, and sustainable manner. While the current focus is on electronic prescriptions, it has been recognized that this should be framed within a broader digital health context, particularly aligned with a Health Information Exchange (HIE) reference architecture. At present, there are several key considerations and challenges in Afghanistan context, including: Lack of clarity on implementation scope and approach (e.g. hospitals vs wider health facilities); Infrastructure constraints in resource-limited settings; Need for interoperability with existing or future digital health systems (e.g. patient records, reporting systems); Data governance, privacy, and security requirements; Capacity and sustainability considerations for long-term system operations. Through this TA request, ACO seeks support from the Health CoE and Global Digital Health expertise to: Provide guidance on how electronic prescription systems should be positioned within a broader Health Information Exchange (HIE) and digital health ecosystem; Share global/UNICEF best practices, country examples (e.g. Jordan and similar contexts), and reference architectures; Advise on phased and realistic implementation approaches suitable for resource-constrained environments; Highlight key technical, governance, interoperability, and data protection considerations; Recommend potential partners or mechanisms for technical exchange and knowledge sharing with MoPH. The objective is to support UNICEF ACO in developing a technically positive and strategic response to MoPH, ensuring alignment with global digital health standards while avoiding fragmented or standalone system implementations. For reference, the related email chain has also been attached for your review. Kindly note that the expected start date is just an estimation and I select a date as it was mandatory field to be filled.

desc: Develop RapidPro fact sheet for Government of Tanzania
full: UNICEF Tanzania requested communications support to develop a briefing note for Government of Tanzania business stakeholders (Ministry of Health and TAMISEMI) on the Afya Yetu / RapidPro platform. Technical alignment between UNICEF and government counterparts was already in place, but a clear, non-technical explanation was needed to address questions around software ownership, licensing costs, and an unexpected appearance of charges that had caused confusion at senior levels. The core message required: that RapidPro is free, open-source software with no licensing fees; that any charges observed were attributable to third-party services (specifically Meta/WhatsApp, an optional channel); and that the Government of Tanzania holds full ownership of the platform, hosted on TAMISEMI and MoH-controlled infrastructure with trained in-house staff. A secondary strategic framing was developed to position RapidPro's longer-term potential as Tanzania's national health communications layer, integrated with the national Health Information Exchange (HIE).

desc: Education Can't Wait proposal
full: I am reaching out to explore whether the Centre of Excellence may be able to provide direct technical surge support to South Sudan for the development of the upcoming Education Cannot Wait Multi-Year Resilience Programme (ECW-MYRP) full proposal. South Sudan has been closely engaged in the development of the MYRP process and country architecture and has played an active role in shaping the programme concept and preparing for the forthcoming call for proposals. We also just concluded the in-country mission of Dianah and the ECW team from 31 May to 5 June, which helped further clarify expectations and momentum around the next phase. We understand that the call for full proposals is expected to be launched in the second half of June. Given the timeline and complexity of the process, we are assessing how best to organize dedicated support for proposal development. We also know the compition in country for this will be very strong, with Save the Children-led consortium having been the grantee for the past 2 rounds. The full proposal will require intensive coordination and technical leadership across several streams simultaneously, including narrative development, results framework design, budgeting, consortium consultations and overall coherence of the programme package. We are currently considering a consortium structure including Oxfam, Humanity & Inclusion, and CINA as a national partner, alongside broader stakeholder engagement. At the same time, our in-country capacity is currently constrained—both within EiE and more broadly across programme teams—and we are concerned about our ability to dedicate sufficient senior technical bandwidth to lead a process of this scale while maintaining ongoing delivery. Before moving to recruit an external consultant, we wanted to check whether CoE may have availability to deploy an experienced colleague or expert to support the process in-country for approximately three weeks. Ideally, this person would lead and facilitate the proposal development process, coordinate consultations across partners, and support drafting of the full package. Someone with deep familiarity with ECW MYRP processes—and, if possible, prior experience in South Sudan or comparable fragile contexts—would be particularly valuable. We recognize this is a significant ask and timelines are short, but we thought it important to explore internal options first before launching external recruitment. Please let us know whether this could be feasible or whether there are alternative support modalities that CoE would recommend. Many thanks in advance for considering this request.

Purpose of the Request: To request technical support from the Adolescent Girls Hub to co-design and deliver a session on “Adolescent Girls as an Accelerator” , as part of the Strategic Plan and regional priorities discussions. The session will aim to: Deepen understanding of adolescent girls as a strategic accelerator within UNICEF’s Strategic Plan and the WCAR regional agenda Demonstrate how investing in adolescent girls drives multisectoral and transformative results Support translation of the accelerator approach into Country Programme Planning processes , including prioritisation and theory of change Scope of Work: Co-design and co-facilitate a 45-minute session (in collaboration with WCARO and Nigeria CO) Present global frameworks, evidence, and programmatic guidance on adolescent girls as an accelerator Illustrate linkages to Strategic Plan accelerators, gender equality priorities, and regional agenda Provide practical examples and country-relevant insights Support participants in understanding how to integrate adolescent girls into CPP components (e.g., evidence synthesis, prioritisation, ToC) Share key tools, resources, and reference materials Dates and Timing: Training Dates: 08–11 June 2026 Session Date: Monday, 8 June 2026 Time: 10:45 AM – 11:30 AM Modality: In-person (Abuja, Nigeria) Expected Outputs: Delivery of a session on Adolescent Girls as an Accelerator Strengthened participant understanding of how to apply the accelerator concept within Rights and Results Programming and CPP processes Session materials and resources shared with participants Participants: Approximately 50 participants from WCARO and Country Offices (Nigeria, Ghana, The Gambia, Guinea-Bissau) Focal Point: Takudzwa Kanyangarara

WCARO, in collaboration with OSE and participating Country Offices (Nigeria, Ghana, The Gambia, and Guinea-Bissau), is convening the Regional (Anglophone) Rights and Results Programming (RRP) Part II Training from 08–11 June 2026 in Abuja, Nigeria. The workshop aims to strengthen staff capacity to design high-quality, rights-based, and results-oriented Country Programmes, with a strong emphasis on practical application across the Country Programme Planning (CPP) cycle. As part of the agenda, a dedicated session on “Adolescent Girls as an Accelerator” is scheduled for Monday, 8 June 2026 (10:45–11:30 AM). The session will be co-facilitated by the Adolescent Girls Hub and UNICEF Nigeria Country Office and will focus on positioning adolescent girls as a strategic accelerator linked to global and regional commitments, including the UNICEF Strategic Plan, Africa Strategy, and WCAR priorities, while demonstrating their role in driving transformative, multisectoral outcomes. The Nigeria Country Office, on behalf of WCARO, is requesting technical support from the Global Gender Equality Team – Adolescent Girls Hub to virtually co-design and co-facilitate this 45-minute session. The session should present key frameworks, evidence, and practical examples, and clearly highlight how adolescent girls can be systematically integrated into Country Programme Planning processes, including evidence synthesis, prioritization, and theory of change. Expected outputs include delivery of the session and sharing of materials to support ongoing application by approximately 50 participants from WCARO and participating Country Offices. The focal point for this request is Takudzwa Kanyangarara.

desc: technical support request to strengthen he capacity of public and private (Small and Medium Entrepreneur) stakeholders in producing quality diets for children 6
full: Strengthening the capacity of public and private (Small and Medium Entrepreneur) stakeholders in producing quality diets for children 6-23 months. Given the poor diet among children in Timor-Leste and the high burden of stunting and following the recommendations of the study on the analysis of barriers and enablers to children's diets 6-23 months, the Government is interested in investing in local and sustainable solutions to improve the quality of children's diets. In the absence of the private sector and with funding support from UNICEF Australia, UNICEF TLCO is partnering with the Tanzania Food and Nutrition Centre (TFNC) to provide technical assistance to SMEs in Timor-Leste to build their capacity to strengthen the food system for sustainable diets for children 6-23 months. Hence, support is needed to UNICEF TLCO on the food system for children, including linking with Mahidol University for nutrient analysis, generating evidence, costing and market model analysis, and reinforcing norms and standards for produced foods, and designing a scalable cash-transfer-for-child diet model. Also, the social marketing of child feeding behaviour. Expected Outcome Facilitate agreement with Mahidol University for nutrient food content analysis (Q3 2026) Establishment of standards for production of complementary foods, aligned with WHO 2023 and CODEX Guidance. (Codex Alimentarius Commission). (Q4 2026) Comprehensive First Foods market and value-chain analysis, including SME landscape, demand patterns, and affordability modelling (Q4 2026) Support on Social Marketing on feeding behaviour campaign (Q1-Q4 2026)

desc: Technica request to develop a concise, visually engaging Programme Synopsis/communication product documenting UNICEF Greece’s National Action against Childhood
full: UNICEF Greece, in partnership with the Hellenic Ministry of Health, has completed the implementation of the National Action against Childhood Obesity (2023–2025) , funded through the EU Recovery and Resilience Facility. The programme encompassed primary, secondary and tertiary prevention interventions targeting children aged 0–17 and their families, spanning home, school, health services and community settings, and engaged a wide range of stakeholders including paediatricians, nutritionists, municipalities and civil society partners. With the programme cycle now concluded, UNICEF Greece is requesting Technical Assistance from the Centre of Excellence to develop a Programme Synopsis/Communication Product — a concise, visually compelling and widely disseminable knowledge product for global UNICEF audiences (including all relevant Country Offices), government counterparts, donors and partners, in coordination with the UNICEF Greece Country Office Programme and Comms team. The document should capture the key strategic shifts achieved, document core programme design parameters , highlight methodologies, tools and approaches developed and applied, and consolidate lessons learnt and good practices in a format suitable for replication in other national contexts. The product will serve as a key outcome document for dissemination through UNICEF's ICON platform and other global knowledge-sharing channels, contributing to UNICEF's broader evidence base on national-level childhood obesity prevention.

desc: Develop Disability inclusive budgeting guidelines
full: This request seeks technical assistance to support the Government of Kenya to develop and operationalize disability inclusive budgeting guidelines that are aligned with national public finance systems, building on recent workshop outcomes that focused on integrating disability into budget cycles, strengthening tagging approaches, and aligning with global commitments such as the Amman Berlin Declaration and the 15 percent target. The support will strengthen systems for planning, allocating, tracking, and reporting disability inclusive expenditure by providing a technical review and consolidation of draft guidelines, ensuring alignment with PFM frameworks, IFMIS and SCOA structures, and international tagging standards while defining clear criteria for disability specific and mainstreamed spending across sectors. It will deliver revised guidelines, an operational framework for integration into the budget cycle, a harmonized tagging methodology, capacity development materials, and an implementation roadmap, while engaging relevant global expertise across public finance, disability inclusion, social protection, and monitoring systems. Through the global support, learning and technical engagement, the request will leverage strategic accelerators including existing tagging systems, alignment with the 2027 to 2028 budget cycle, adaptation of gender and child budgeting practices, strong government ownership, structured engagement with organizations of persons with disabilities, and coordinated support from development partners to ensure high quality and rapidly implementable results.

desc: Climate Resilience, Climate Action and Sustainability Training for ZCO
full: TA Request: Climate Resilience, Climate Action and Sustainability Training for ZCO Short Description of the Request Support: CO will lead; CoE is requested to join sessions as backstop This Technical Assistance (TA) request seeks to design and facilitate a tailored two-session training for UNICEF Zambia Country Office (ZCO) staff on Module 2 in Climate Resilience, Climate Action, and Sustainability. The training will strengthen staff capacity to integrate climate-responsive programming, risk-informed planning, and sustainability principles across sectors. The training will be delivered over two half-day sessions: 29 July (09:00–12:00) 30 July (14:00–17:00) It will combine practical tools, global best practices, and Zambia-specific contextualization to ensure applicability to ongoing and future programmes. After completing Module 2, learners will be better able to: Co-create, with colleagues from multiple sectors: 1) a causality flowchart for the country, tracing climate change impacts on children and youth, and 2) a product to help mainstream climate resilience and action with and for children, e.g. an infographic, resource list, narrative Describe the difference between primary, secondary and cascading hazards and impacts Research the climate risks and hazards in your country using online resources Give sectoral examples of direct and indirect climate impacts on children and youth Explain how children experience the impacts of climate change disproportionately by describing at least four types of their distinct vulnerabilities Explain how adolescent girls are particularly exposed to climate and environmental hazards considering the underlying vulnerabilities they live with Use multiple sources to discover and describe opportunities for children and youth in your country to be agents of change in climate resilience and action, e.g. breaking the harmful vulnerability-exposure loop, taking leadership roles in climate governance and finance Analyze a participation opportunity for children and youth for its level of engagement Identify key stakeholders and partners to consult with on climate resilience and climate action

desc: CC4C: Development of an Adolescent Climate Action Engagement Strategy
full: Request for Technical Support: Development of an Adolescent Climate Action Engagement Strategy UNICEF Malawi is seeking technical support from the Centre of Excellence to develop an Adolescent Climate Action Engagement Strategy that will provide a coherent framework for adolescent engagement in climate action programming. Climate change is increasingly affecting the lives and futures of adolescents in Malawi, particularly adolescent girls who face heightened vulnerabilities related to education, health, livelihoods, and protection. In response, UNICEF Malawi has been supporting a range of climate action initiatives involving both in-school and out-of-school adolescents. These interventions have included climate awareness raising, climate-smart livelihoods, environmental conservation activities, leadership development, advocacy, and adolescent participation in climate-related platforms. While these efforts have generated valuable results, they have evolved through different programme streams and partnerships without an overarching strategic framework to guide and harmonize adolescent climate engagement. As a result, there is a need to develop a clear strategy that articulates UNICEF Malawi's vision, priorities, approaches, and expected results for adolescent climate action. The proposed technical support would assist UNICEF Malawi to: • Review existing adolescent climate action initiatives and lessons learned; • Assess opportunities and gaps in adolescent engagement in climate action and resilience-building; • Define a strategic framework for engaging adolescents, with particular attention to adolescent girls and other vulnerable groups; • Identify evidence-based approaches for strengthening adolescent leadership, participation, advocacy, and climate resilience; • Develop a results framework and implementation roadmap; • Ensure alignment with UNICEF's global and regional climate strategies, the Malawi Country Programme, and national climate policies and priorities. The strategy will support UNICEF Malawi in moving from fragmented climate-related activities towards a more intentional, evidence-based, and scalable approach to adolescent climate action, positioning adolescents as agents of change while strengthening their resilience to climate-related shocks and stresses. related term: CC4C

desc: Measles Outbreak Root Cause Analysis and Immunization Systems Strengthening Support
full: Technical Assistance Request: Capacity Building and Root Cause Analysis for Measles Outbreaks 1. Title Capacity Building of UNICEF Staff and Facilitation of Root Cause Analysis (RCA) for Measles Outbreaks in High-Burden States 2. Background and Justification In 2026, India has experienced high burden of Measles cases and outbreaks. Within the first five months of 2026, more than 19,800 cases of measles have been reported across the country which have surpassed the total number of 17,800 cases reported in the entire year of 2025. With high reported administrative coverages of MCV, these cases and outbreaks highlight persistent gaps in routine immunization systems, surveillance, and outbreak response capacity. Despite ongoing immunization efforts, outbreaks continue to occur due to a combination of systemic, programmatic, and contextual factors. Root Cause Analysis (RCA) is a structured approach that helps identify underlying causes contributing to outbreaks, beyond surface-level factors. Strengthening the capacity of UNICEF staff at country and field offices to conduct RCA will enable systematic identification of bottlenecks in immunization service delivery, surveillance, demand generation, and program management. Furthermore, conducting RCA exercises in high-burden states will generate context-specific evidence to inform targeted action plans. These action plans are expected to strengthen immunization systems and contribute to reducing the burden of vaccine-preventable diseases, particularly measles. 3. Objectives General Objective To strengthen the capacity of UNICEF staff and support evidence-based action planning through Root Cause Analysis of measles outbreaks. Specific Objectives Build technical capacity of UNICEF country office and field office staff to plan and conduct RCA of measles outbreaks. Facilitate comprehensive RCA exercises in two states with high measles burden in 2026. Support development of actionable, evidence-based plans to strengthen immunization systems. Promote integration of RCA findings into routine immunization and outbreak response strategies. 4. Scope of Work The TA will support the following key activities: 4.1 Capacity Building Develop/adapt RCA training materials tailored to the immunization context. Conduct training workshop for UNICEF staff (Health & SBC teams) at country and field levels. Provide practical guidance on RCA tools, methodologies, and data interpretation. 4.2 Facilitation of RCA in Two High-Burden States Facilitate planning and execution of RCA exercises, including: Data review (surveillance, immunization coverage, outbreak response) Stakeholder consultations (health officials, frontline workers, communities) Field assessments Apply standardized RCA frameworks (e.g., fishbone analysis, problem tree analysis). 4.3 Development of Action Plans Support state teams to translate RCA findings into targeted action plans. Ensure plans address key system gaps (e.g., service delivery, cold chain, demand generation, data quality). Define clear timelines, responsibilities, and monitoring indicators. 4.4 Documentation and Knowledge Sharing Document RCA findings, lessons learned, and best practices. Develop a summary report and guidance note for wider dissemination. 5. Expected Deliverables Adapted RCA training package and tools. Capacity-building sessions conducted for UNICEF staff. RCA reports for two high-burden states. State-specific action plans to strengthen immunization systems. Final TA report summarizing findings, recommendations, and lessons learned. 6. Timeline Proposed duration: 3–4 months Activity Timeline Preparation and tool adaptation Weeks 1–2 Capacity building workshops Week 2 RCA in two states Weeks 3-5 Action plan development Weeks 5–7 Reporting and dissemination Weeks 8-10 7. Resource Requirements Technical expert(s) with experience in: Immunization systems strengthening Measles outbreak investigation Root Cause Analysis methodologies Budget for: Training workshops (travel, venue, materials) Field visits for data collection in two states Workshops for development of action plans Documentation and reporting 8. Expected Outcomes Enhanced capacity of UNICEF staff to independently conduct RCA. Improved understanding of drivers of measles outbreaks in high-burden states. Development of targeted, evidence-based interventions. Strengthened immunization systems, contributing to reduced incidence of measles and other vaccine-preventable diseases. 9. Monitoring and Evaluation Number of staff trained on RCA methodologies. Completion of RCA exercises in selected states. Quality and implementation status of developed action plans. Evidence of integration of RCA findings into program strategies. 10. Request for Technical Assistance UNICEF ICO seeks technical support to: Design and deliver RCA capacity-building activities. Facilitate RCA exercises in identified states. Guide development of actionable immunization strengthening plans.

desc: Lebanon is facing a severe humanitarian crisis with widespread displacement, affecting children and caregivers' access to nutrition, early childhood development
full: Lebanon is facing a severe and escalating humanitarian crisis, with the most recent shocks resulting in the displacement of an estimated 10–20 per cent of the population. Many displaced families are now living in precarious and temporary accommodation, including collective shelters, tents, unfinished or overcrowded rented housing, and with host families. These conditions have had a profound impact on children and caregivers, severely disrupting diets, access to essential nutrition and early childhood development (ECD) services, and caregiving practices for infants, young children, adolescent girls, and pregnant and breastfeeding women. Widespread displacement, economic hardship, and insecurity are placing intense pressure on families’ ability to provide adequate nutrition and nurturing care. Children are growing up in environments characterized by instability, overcrowding, limited privacy, and poor conditions for food preparation, storage, hygiene, play, and early stimulation. Heightened caregiver stress, poverty, repeated disruption, and the erosion of family and community support systems are increasing risks of malnutrition, inappropriate feeding practices, and long‑term developmental harm. Caregivers face mounting barriers, including limited access to diverse and nutritious foods; unsafe and unsolicited donations of breastmilk substitutes and ultra‑processed foods; and reduced opportunities for breastfeeding, responsive feeding, and nurturing care. Disruptions to routine health, nutrition, and ECD services further undermine families’ capacity to sustain appropriate diets and caregiving practices during this period of acute vulnerability. In response, UNICEF, in close coordination with the Ministry of Public Health (MoPH) and Nutrition Sector partners, is implementing an integrated, life‑cycle nutrition response to protect child survival, growth, and development. This includes infant and young child feeding (IYCF) and ECD counselling, wasting screening and treatment, preventive and emergency nutrition supplies, nutrition risk communication, protection of breastfeeding through regulation of breastmilk substitutes, and nutrition surveillance, delivered through health, community, education, and digital platforms. As the Nutrition Sector/Cluster lead and main technical partner for nutrition and ECD in Lebanon, UNICEF provides technical leadership, strengthens frontline capacity, ensures continuity of essential supplies, supports coordination and information management, and maintains last‑resort service delivery where gaps persist. Within this context, short‑term technical assistance is required to support the operationalization of new capacity‑strengthening roles, consolidate nutrition education across the life course, develop initial technical guidance for emerging response modalities, and strengthen nutrition advocacy and resource mobilization to support the strategic design, coherence, and operational readiness of the integrated Nutrition and Child Development emergency response in a rapidly evolving crisis context with particular emphasis on emergency financing, sector coordination, and technical guidance for emerging response modalities.

desc: Big Catch-Up Dose Reconciliation and Reporting Support for Nepal
full: Title : Technical Assistance Request for Big Catch-Up Dose Reconciliation and Reporting in Nepal Description Nepal is implementing the Big Catch-Up (BCU) initiative with Gavi-supported doses to reach missed children. As per updated Gavi guidance, dose reconciliation is a mandatory process comparing BCU doses delivered with doses administered (including wastage) to ensure accountability and proper use of resources. The reconciliation exercise will be conducted based on cumulative doses administered (through 2025 or up to March 2026 where applicable) and reported through standardized monitoring and reconciliation forms. Countries must also report detailed data including doses delivered, doses administered by antigen, stock levels, and wastage rates, forming the basis for validation and performance assessment. Where significant unused doses remain, these may be reclassified to routine immunization, potentially reducing future Gavi-supported allocations without affecting country co-financing obligations. Given these requirements, UNICEF Nepal seeks technical support to institutionalize robust reconciliation, reporting, and risk management processes. Expected Output Functional Dose Reconciliation System Standardized tools and methodology aligned with the BCU Dose Reconciliation Form, capturing doses delivered, administered (by antigen), wastage, and stock levels. Clear processes for compiling cumulative reporting and ensuring readiness for Q1/Q2 2026 reconciliation timelines. Strengthened Reporting and Reclassification Preparedness Consolidated reporting templates and validation processes to ensure accurate and complete BCU reporting across all antigens. Guidance for managing leftover doses, risk thresholds, and reclassification implications on future allocations , including scenario-based planning. This TA will enable Nepal to ensure credible reconciliation of BCU doses, compliance with Gavi requirements, and mitigation of financial and programmatic risks.

full: Haiti Solarization Assessment TA (HCF) UNICEF Haiti is seeking targeted technical assistance to conduct a rapid technical review and validation of the solarization assessment of Health Care Facilities (HCFs), with the objective of informing regional (LACRO) prepositioning strategies for solar energy solutions in health systems. The request builds on an ongoing national solarization needs assessment initiated in 2025, where theoretical training has been completed and field deployment is underway. The TA will support quality assurance of assessment data, validation of methodology/tools, and translation of findings into actionable recommendations for scalable solarization interventions in Haiti and across the LAC region. Given the time-sensitive funding window (expiring in December) and ongoing field activities, rapid, field-oriented support is critical to ensure the assessment is finalized to a high technical standard and can inform procurement and strategic decisions. Objectives and Expected Outcomes Overall Objective Ensure that the solarization assessment of HCFs in Haiti is technically robust, operationally relevant, and usable for regional decision-making and prepositioning. Specific Objectives Technical Validation of the Assessment Review and validate the proper application of the solarization assessment tool for HCFs (HFSE/EAT). Ensure consistency, accuracy, and standardization across all data collection efforts. Deployment of Field-Based Technical Assistance (Special Mission) Mobilize a specialist with proven experience in the HCF solarization assessment tool to undertake a one-week special mission to Haiti . During the mission, the specialist will: Complete the practical, in-country field training for Ministry of Health (MoH) and UNICEF teams. Accompany teams during field visits to selected health facilities to ensure correct use of the assessment tool and provide real-time troubleshooting and guidance. This responds to the identified gap between completed theoretical training and the need for practical application prior to full rollout. Quality Assurance During Nationwide Deployment Provide r emote technical backstopping following the mission to support field teams deployed across the 10 departments of the country. desc: Support effective state reform
full: During the recent visit of Ted Chaiban and Roberto Benes to Venezuela, the Venezuela’s Vice President for Social and Territorial Socialism of Venezuela - Héctor Rodríguez referred to his recent appointment as Presidential Commissioner for the Restructuring and Reengineering of the National Government. He explained that this assignment involves a government-led review of ministries and public entities, with the objective of optimizing public resources, streamlining administrative processes and assessing the relevance and possible merger of public bodies under a broader logic of simplification and improved efficiency of the State. In this context, he requested UNICEF’s technical support in identifying relevant international experiences, models and good practices from countries that have undertaken effective state reform or public administration modernization processes. The interest is not in UNICEF advising on specific institutional decisions in Venezuela, but rather in helping the Government access comparative evidence, analytical frameworks and lessons learned that could inform the design and conduct of such a review. Overall the VP would need evidence of comparative country experiences where child related state reform or public administration modernization has shown improved efficiency, coordination and service delivery. In particular: Effective ways to ensure that simplification or efficiency measures do not weaken essential social services, particularly those affecting children and vulnerable populations. Suggestions to improve the relevance, performance, and reduce overlap or fragmentation of child related ministries, agencies and public entities. This includes institutional arrangements that have helped improve coordination across social sectors, reduce duplication and strengthen accountability. Finally, possible links between state modernization, public finance for children and improved delivery of basic services, especially in commodity rich/commodity depending countries. What has worked, where and why?”

desc: MCH Data Systems, Child Mortality Statistics and Indicator Review Support for China
full: UNICEF China is preparing a proposed 2026–2027 workstream with the Department of Maternal and Child Health, National Health Commission of China, on MCH data, indicator system review and child mortality statistics. The workstream aims to support government partners to review and optimize the existing maternal and child health statistical indicator system, improve child mortality statistics in a low-mortality setting, and strengthen routine data quality and use for policy and programme decision-making. China already has a well-established MCH data and reporting system, which has supported major progress in maternal, neonatal, infant and under-five mortality reduction. However, as mortality continues to decline, the policy agenda is shifting from a primarily survival-focused agenda towards broader child health, development, service quality, continuity of care, equity and adolescent health. The proposed workstream will therefore examine whether the current MCH indicator system remains fit for purpose, which indicators should be retained, refined, retired or added/linked, and how relevant data sources can be better connected. The proposed government-owned workstream is expected to involve three national technical institutions: the National MCH Annual Reporting Office / Peking University Health Science Center, the National Office for Maternal and Child Health Surveillance, and the NHC Statistical Information Center. They are currently refining the detailed proposal, collaboration mechanism, institutional responsibilities, workplan and budget. This TA request is submitted at the proposal preparation stage. UNICEF China is not requesting a large technical mission at this stage. The request is for light-touch, time-bound technical advice, relevant global tools/examples, and later review of the draft proposal once available. The specific areas where technical advice would be useful are: Indicator system review and life-course child health measurement, including global experience and tools for reviewing MNCAH, child and adolescent health indicator systems in settings moving from survival-focused measurement towards broader child health and development measurement. Child mortality statistics, data linkage and data quality assurance, including child mortality measurement in low-mortality settings, subnational interpretation, data triangulation, child death reporting, linkage with birth/death registration and routine health data, and good practices in routine data quality assurance. Responsible use of AI and advanced analytics in routine health data systems, including realistic and responsible applications for data quality checks, anomaly detection, duplicate or missing case identification, cause-of-death coding support, data linkage, dashboard development and policy-oriented interpretation, with appropriate validation, governance, privacy protection and human oversight. An initial discussion with CoE/OSE colleagues has already taken place on June 18, 2026. Charles Nwosisi and colleagues advised that China may have an opportunity to serve as a front runner in exploring how MCH data systems can evolve from a survival-focused agenda towards broader child health and development measurement. They also advised UNICEF China to make the request specific and log it through REACH as a light-touch, time-bound TA request.

The rollout in Fiji is being implemented through a phased, multi-channel and multi-sectoral approach, leveraging government systems, service providers, and community networks to drive adoption and sustained engagement. To support effective implementation, we would appreciate technical assistance in the following areas: SBC and demand generation: Guidance on optimizing behaviourally informed strategies to move caregivers from awareness to sustained app use, including strengthening provider referral pathways and community-based promotion. Service delivery integration: Support to embed Bebbo within routine interactions across health, social protection, and early childhood services, including tools for frontline workers and training/refresher approaches. Monitoring and analytics: Technical guidance on tracking user engagement, analysing app usage data, and applying insights to refine rollout strategies in real time. Content and localization: Advice on further tailoring and translation of content (including language adaptation and cultural relevance) and identifying priority gaps based on caregiver needs and feedback. Scale-up and sustainability: Support on approaches for phased geographic expansion (urban, rural, and maritime settings), partnership strengthening, and long-term institutionalization within national systems. Fiji has already initiated key rollout components including communications activities, partner engagement, and service provider outreach aligned with national priorities for early childhood development and parenting support. The TA support will be critical in ensuring quality implementation, accelerating uptake, and sustaining impact at scale.

desc: Integrated Cold Chain, Biomedical Equipment and PHC Maintenance Systems Strengthening Support for Malawi
full: Request for integrated PHC equipment maintenance support in Malawi: With the establishment of Cold Chain Technician Teams (CCTs) in all districts in Malawi, and deployment of toolkits and spare parts, maintenance capacity exists in Malawi — but is limited to CCE and not integrated across PHC systems. In addition to the TA towards the planned EVMA, MCO would like to request for TA to leverage the Lilongwe Technical College as a potential training hub for technicians, not only on cold chain systems but also on broader biomedical and PHC-related equipment. The request seeks technical assistance to strengthen national and sub-national capacity for preventive and corrective maintenance of Cold Chain Equipment (CCE) and other critical biomedical equipment supplied through LTAs. Despite significant investments in equipment procurement, gaps remain in maintenance skills, availability of trained technicians, and systems for timely repair—resulting in equipment downtime and risks to vaccine potency and service delivery. The TA will support development and implementation of standardized training, maintenance systems, and supervision approaches to improve equipment functionality, reduce downtime, and enhance quality of immunization and primary health care services. As it stands: Maintenance currently operates in parallel silos: -Cold chain -Infrastructure -WASH systems -Oxygen systems In an environment of limited: -Multi-skilled technicians -Integrated planning and budgeting -Lifecycle management frameworks Overall Objective Strengthen national and sub-national capacity to ensure sustainable functionality, maintenance, and optimal performance of CCE and biomedical equipment to support uninterrupted service delivery for children. Specific Objectives Build technical capacity: Strengthen knowledge and practical skills of health workers and technicians in preventive and corrective maintenance of CCE and priority biomedical equipment. Establish functional maintenance systems: Support development/strengthening of national and sub-national maintenance frameworks, SOPs, and workflows for timely fault detection, reporting, and repair. Improve equipment uptime and performance: Reduce frequency and duration of equipment breakdowns through structured maintenance practices and availability of tools and spare parts. Strengthen data visibility and accountability: Enhance tracking of equipment functionality, maintenance needs, and response times using digital tools and monitoring systems. Promote sustainability: Institutionalize training and maintenance approaches within MoH systems, including integration into existing technical training institutions and supervision structures. Milestones: 1. Assessment (inventory, workflows, etc) & resource mapping 2. System integration design of the Integrated Maintenance Model 3. Capacity Building including capacitating Lilongwe Technical College, curricula adaptation and upskill capacity enhancement for existing CCTs to PHC maintenance technicians 4. Development of tools, systems & initial implementation support This TA will contribute to improved vaccine potency, reduced equipment downtime, and strengthened primary health care delivery, ultimately supporting equitable access to life-saving services for children.

desc: Cold Chain Temperature Mapping and Vaccine Quality Assurance Support for Malawi
full: Malawi Country Office seeks technical assistance to conduct a comprehensive temperature mapping study of vaccine cold chain equipment across selected storage sites in Malawi. While cold chain infrastructure has expanded significantly, evidence gaps remain regarding temperature distribution, equipment performance, and compliance with storage standards. The mapping study will generate critical data to identify risks (e.g., freezing, hotspots, poor air circulation), inform corrective actions, and strengthen maintenance and equipment placement practices. The TA will support improved vaccine quality assurance and contribute to enhanced immunization service delivery. Overall Objective Ensure optimal temperature performance of cold chain equipment to safeguard vaccine potency and improve the quality of immunization services. Specific Objectives Assess temperature performance of CCE: Conduct detailed temperature mapping of selected cold rooms, refrigerators, and freezers to identify spatial temperature variations. Identify risks affecting vaccine quality: Detect hotspots, cold spots, freezing risks, and distribution irregularities within storage equipment. Strengthen evidence-based decision-making: Provide actionable recommendations for equipment use, loading practices, maintenance, and placement. Enhance quality assurance systems: Support integration of temperature mapping findings into routine supervision, SOPs, and EVM improvement plans. Build national capacity: Develop local capacity for periodic temperature mapping, interpretation of results, and corrective actions. Milestones: Inception & planning completed: Protocol, sites, tools, and implementation plan finalised. Data collection conducted: Temperature loggers deployed and data gathered across selected sites. Analysis completed: Temperature variations, risks (hotspots/freezing), and compliance assessed. Reporting & validation finalized: Study report validated with stakeholders and action plan agreed. Capacity building & integration achieved: Staff trained and findings integrated into SOPs, monitoring, and maintenance systems.

desc: CC4C: Scaling Youth-led Green Start-ups and Organizations under Youth Challenge Green Generation 2025
full: TA Request: Scaling Youth-led Green Start-ups and Organizations under Youth Challenge Green Generation 2025 (CC4C – Deliverable 2) The country office requests Technical Assistance (TA) from the CoE under the Climate Collaboration for Children (CC4C), Output 1 – Deliverable 2, to implement the following activities to support and scale youth-led green start-ups and concrete climate action initiatives emerging from the Green Desafio Genial programme. Building on last year’s cohort (see more information on the Youth Challenge below), the TA will work with 5–10 youth-led start-ups from the Youth Challenge, and additionally 3–5 existing local youth-let climate and environment CSOs. The aim is to advance and support these organizations and start-ups in scaling, with practical training and support sessions. In line with CC4C priorities, the initiative will also apply a Participatory Action Research (PAR) approach to strengthen youth capacity in data-driven implementation, monitoring, and local evidence generation, contributing to community-level awareness and stakeholder engagement. Online capacity building workshop and mentoring programme : Design and deliver a structured online capacity-building programme for the selected youth-led green innovation teams participating in Youth Challenge (Desafio Genial 2025 – Geração Verde). The programme will: strengthen participants' entrepreneurial and innovation skills through practical workshops and coaching sessions focused on: Business models canvas, (value proposition, customer segments), financial sustainability strategies, operations and delivery models, market research and analysis, environmental and social impact measurement, and improving on their product for better sustainability. The programme will combine expert-led sessions, peer learning, and mentoring support to help teams transform innovative ideas into feasible and sustainable green enterprises or climate action initiatives. In-person green innovation bootcamp and pilot readiness workshop to complement the online workshop with practical sessions and a strong pilot-readiness component). Organize a 5-day in-person workshop in Luanda, featuring hands-on sessions designed to strengthen participants’ entrepreneurial and innovation capacities. The bootcamp will combine practical workshops and targeted coaching sessions, with a focus on: Business models canvas, (value proposition, customer segments), financial sustainability strategies, operations and delivery models, market research and analysis, environmental and social impact measurement, and improving on their product for better sustainability. The workshop will culminate in the preparation of pilot-ready interventions that can be tested within communities, schools, or local ecosystems, generating evidence for future scaling and investment opportunities. The programme will combine expert-led sessions, peer learning, and mentoring support to help teams transform innovative ideas into feasible and sustainable green enterprises or climate action initiatives. Financial support to legal registration, proto-types and pilot projects : A financial component to support the operationalization and sustainability of selected youth-led green start-ups and CSOs in their start-up. This will cover business formalization, legal registration and compliance costs, as well as financial support to develop proto-type and pilot-scale project. Estimated budget: USD 40,000. Background (Youth Challenge): UNICEF Angola, through Generation Unlimited (GenU), has been implementing Desafio Genial since 2024 , a national innovation challenge that promotes youth entrepreneurship and problem-solving skills. The 2025 edition, Desafio Genial – Geração Verde , focuses on climate resilience, environmental sustainability, and green entrepreneurship. The initiative received more than 1,500 applications from young people from across Angola. Following a competitive selection process, 200 teams were shortlisted, and 20 teams advanced to the pre-bootcamp stage. Out of those 20 teams, 4 winners were chosen and won the Challenge. The challenge aims to identify and support innovative youth-led solutions addressing climate and environmental challenges, including waste management, renewable energy, climate-smart agriculture, circular economy, water management, and community resilience. While the challenge has successfully mobilized young innovators, there is a need to strengthen the incubation and implementation phase to ensure that promising ideas evolve into sustainable and scalable green enterprises and community-based climate solutions. Expected Outcome: At least 5-10 start-ups and 3-5 CSO’s equipped during the capacity building programme with entrepreneurial and innovation skills. At least 5 youth-led green initiatives will develop validated business models and implementation plans, launch pilot interventions and progress towards sustainable and scalable climate-resilient enterprises.

desc: National Vaccination Forum Participation and Gavi 6.0 Roadmap Support for Mauritania
full: Requête pour mission de staff – Contribution aux débats du Forum National de la Vaccination en Mauritanie et suivi de la mise en œuvre de la soumission GAVI 6.0 Date : 6-7 juillet 2026 Forum /8juillet 2026 Suivi feuille de route soumission GAVI 6.0 1. Contexte et justification Dans le cadre du renforcement du Programme Élargi de Vaccination (PEV) et en préparation des engagements nationaux liés aux financements durables et pérennes de vaccination, la Mauritanie organise un forum national sur la vaccination. Ce forum constitue une opportunité stratégique pour : Analyser les progrès et défis du programme de vaccination, Mobiliser les partenaires techniques et financiers, Plaidoyer pour lever des fonds domestiques pour compenser les diminutions de fonds de GAVI Renforcer les orientations stratégiques pour atteindre les populations non ou insuffisamment vaccinées, notamment les enfants « zéro dose ». L’UNICEF, en tant que partenaire clé du PEV, joue un rôle déterminant dans l’appui technique, stratégique et opérationnel, notamment sur les thématiques liées à l’équité vaccinale, le renforcement de la chaine d’approvisionnement des vaccins et chaine de froid. 2. Objectif de la mission Contribuer de manière active et pertinente aux débats de haute qualité du forum, en mettant l’accent sur : L’identification et la réduction des enfants zéro dose, Le renforcement de la stratégie nationale de vaccination, Les mécanismes de financement durable de la vaccination, En parallèle au forum le haut responsable discutera avec les parties prenantes nationales et l’équipe GAVI et les équipes des deux agences OMS/UNICEF sur l’importance de synergie d’effort pour le suivi et la mise en œuvre de la feuille de route de la soumission GAVI 6.0 de manière collégiale et harmonisée. 3. Objectifs spécifiques Analyser et alimenter les discussions sur la problématique des enfants zéro dose : Identification des zones et populations à risque, Approches communautaires et stratégies d’équité, Expériences et contributions de l’UNICEF. Apporter un éclairage sur le financement de la vaccination : Analyse des ressources existantes, Durabilité financière et transition GAVI, Plaidoyer pour l’augmentation des ressources domestiques. Appuyer le suivi de la feuille de route GAVI 6.0 : Identification des priorités nationales, Suivi des engagements et jalons clés, Contribution à la qualité de la soumission. 4. Résultats attendus À l’issue du forum, les résultats suivants sont attendus : Contributions techniques documentées aux différentes sessions, Recommandations concrètes sur la réduction des enfants zéro dose, Orientations claires pour le financement durable, Feuille de route GAVI 6.0 renforcée et alignée avec les priorités nationales. 5. Rôle de l’UNICEF L’UNICEF apportera un appui à travers : Le partage de données et d’analyses sur les enfants zéro dose, L’appui technique aux stratégies d’équité, Le renforcement des approches communautaires, Le soutien au plaidoyer pour un financement durable, L’accompagnement du processus de soumission GAVI 6.0. 6. Modalités de mise en œuvre Participation active aux panels et groupes de travail, Préparation de notes techniques sur les thématiques clés, Coordination avec le ministère de la Santé et les partenaires, Synthèse des recommandations issues des débats

desc: CC4C: Youth Skills Development and Employment
full: The Ethiopia country office requests TA to support and scale an integrated, cross-regional initiative linking Youth Skills Development and Employment under the Mastercard Foundation Jobs Portfolio in Afar, Amhara, and Tigray with School Environmental Clubs in Benishangul-Gumuz (BG), contributing to Deliverable 2: 180 green start-ups supported by UNICEF through the development of concrete, youth-led green livelihood and entrepreneurship pathways. This initiative will also build on work UNICEF has delivered on urban gardening initiatives that support youth- led urban gardening initiatives. By integrating urban gardening into entrepreneurship pathways, youth can develop small-scale businesses that contribute to improved nutrition outcomes while strengthening climate-resilient livelihoods. Urban gardening can also create opportunities to link production, consumption, and markets at community level, reinforcing both sustainable food systems and youth economic empowerment. Specifically, and as part of the Climate Collaboration for Children (CC4C) programme, the TA will support the design and delivery of a cross-regional workshop hosted at a secondary school in BG with a strong environmental club, bringing together school leaders and education and agriculture stakeholders from Afar, Amhara, and Tigray. This will serve as a platform to cross-pollinate ideas, share best practices, and identify scalable models linking climate action, education, and youth employment. Building on the workshop, the TA will support the development of a concrete strategy to scale these approaches, including a clear operational plan and financing strategy to expand youth-led green enterprises across regions. The TA will also undertake a mission to Ethiopia to engage directly with programme sites, contribute technical input to the workshop, and lead or support the development of the strategy, ensuring it is action-oriented, evidence-based, and positioned for scale, including in the lead-up to COP. The Ethiopia country office is bidding TA to be funded by CC4C and10k of finance, which if available this will be used to support the scaling of youth-led green enterprises with particular support for those led by disadvantaged groups. The project is integrated with Ethiopian Government strategies and will be publicized in the run up to COP 32 with lessons learned and finance mobilized to scale successful elements.

desc: Root Cause Analysis and Social Behaviour Change Support for Measles Outbreak Prevention and Response
full: Technical Assistance to Strengthen Root Cause Analysis with SBC Perspective for Measles Outbreak Response in India, with Focused Support to Jharkhand and Rajasthan Requested Expert: Rudrajit Das Description: UNICEF India seeks technical assistance to strengthen the Social and Behaviour Change perspective in the Root Cause Analysis of measles outbreaks in India, with specific implementation support to Rajasthan. The TA will help identify behavioural, social, community, service-delivery and system-level factors contributing to measles transmission, missed vaccination, delayed care-seeking, misinformation, low risk perception and weak community engagement. The support will help ICO and state teams translate RCA findings into a practical SBC/RCCE action plan for Rajasthan, aligned with outbreak response, routine immunization strengthening and government systems. Objectives / Expectations Integrate a strong SBC lens into the measles RCA process, tools and analysis. Identify key behavioural, social, trust-related, access and service-quality barriers contributing to missed or delayed measles vaccination. Support Rajasthan in converting RCA findings into a time-bound SBC/RCCE implementation plan. Build the capacity of UNICEF, government and partner teams to use RCA findings for evidence-based community engagement and demand generation. Ensure that the response is equity-focused, gender-responsive, locally owned and aligned with government and partner coordination mechanisms. Expected Deliverables Refined RCA tools/checklists with SBC questions for caregivers, frontline workers, supervisors, community leaders and local influencers. Simple analysis framework covering demand barriers, access barriers, trust issues, misinformation, gender/social norms and service-delivery gaps. Rajasthan-specific SBC/RCCE action plan linked to outbreak response and routine immunization. Orientation session for UNICEF, government and partner teams on applying SBC within measles RCA. Short learning note with key findings, implementation lessons and recommendations for replication in other states.

desc: Child Health Financing, Service Pricing and Institutionalization Advisory Support
full: UNICEF China is preparing a proposed 2026–2027 workstream with the Department of Maternal and Child Health, National Health Commission of China, on child health service pricing and sustainable financing pathways. The workstream aims to support the institutionalization of selected UNICEF-supported child health interventions by exploring how they can be more clearly defined, costed, priced and linked to sustainable domestic financing mechanisms. The proposed study will focus on three areas already included in the UNICEF–NHC workplan: Early Childhood Development (ECD) services delivered through primary healthcare platforms; Early Essential Newborn Care (EENC) and prematurity-related services; Child health management services. Preliminary discussions with government partners indicate that the study should not be framed as a narrow pricing exercise. In the Chinese policy context, there are several linked questions: whether a service should be recognized as a defined service item or service package; how the service should be costed and priced; whether and how the service can be linked to existing public financing or payment mechanisms. Different services may require different pathways. Some services may be strengthened through the existing Basic Public Health Service Package, while others may need to be considered through medical service pricing or other financing arrangements. This TA request is submitted at the proposal preparation stage. UNICEF China is not requesting a large mission at this stage. The request is for light-touch, time-bound technical advice, relevant global examples, and review of the draft proposal once available. Technical support would be useful in three areas: Global evidence and country experience on financing, purchasing and institutionalization of child health, newborn care, ECD and preventive/promotive health services. Technical advice on study design and methodology, including how to analyse service definition, purchasing arrangements, financing pathways, costing and pricing within a broader health financing framework. Expert inputs and light review of the draft proposal, including advice on research questions, analytical approaches and policy relevance. An introductory discussion has already taken place with UNICEF Health Financing colleagues. Key advice received was that the work should first understand the purchasing landscape, government appetite and financing pathways before focusing on costing tools or pricing methodologies. UNICEF China will continue refining the proposal with government partners and will seek targeted technical review as the work progresses.
